texts.title: Picatrix
texts.description: The Latin Picatrix is the principal medieval Latin witness to the Arabic Ghayat al-hakim and a central source for astral image magic.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Picatrix is the most sophisticated and influential astrological magic text of the medieval and early modern periods. Originally composed in Arabic as the Ghāyat al-ḥakīm (Goal of the Wise), probably in Andalusia around 1000 CE and attributed to the Pseudo-Majriti (the mathematician Maslama al-Majriti was sometimes named), it was translated into Castilian in 1256 under Alfonso X of Castile and from Castilian into Latin around 1300. The Latin translation circulated widely through the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, and portions of it were used by Marsilio Ficino, copied into miscellanies alongside the Clavicula Salomonis, and drawn on by Cornelius Agrippa in De occulta philosophia.

Contents

The Picatrix is organized in four books covering: the principles of astrological magic and celestial influence (Book I); the practical construction of talismans and images keyed to the planets and fixed stars (Book II); more advanced planetary magic, fumigations, suffumigations, and the manipulation of planetary spirits (Book III); and a theoretical treatment of the soul, the world-spirit (pneuma), and the philosophical principles underlying magical efficacy (Book IV). The text draws on Arabic astrology, Neoplatonic philosophy, Hermetic cosmology, and practical ritual traditions to produce a comprehensive system of astral magic that is both theoretically sophisticated and practically detailed.

The talismanic procedures are keyed to the twenty-eight lunar mansions as well as the seven planets, providing a very fine temporal and astrological grid for magical operations. The text specifies the materials (metals, plants, stones, fumigations) appropriate to each celestial power, the images to be inscribed or cast, and the invocations to be used. Its treatment of planetary spirits — as intermediary agents between the celestial bodies and terrestrial matter — is the most elaborate in medieval Latin magical literature.

Scholarship

The critical edition of the Latin text is by David Pingree (2 vols., Warburg Institute, 1986); Pingree's introduction is the essential guide to the text's sources and manuscript tradition. An English translation by John Michael Greer and Christopher Warnock appeared in 2010 (Adocentyn Press) and a more recent scholarly translation with apparatus has been produced by Attrell and Porreca (Penn State, 2019). The Arabic text has been edited by Hellmut Ritter (Leipzig, 1933). For the relationship of the Picatrix to Latin natural philosophy and to Ficino, see Brian Copenhaver's articles and the relevant sections of Weill-Parot's work on addressative magic.

texts.title: Ars Notoria
texts.description: The Ars Notoria is a ritual art of memory and learning transmitted in medieval Latin manuscripts.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Ars Notoria (Notory Art) is a Latin magical text, probably compiled in the twelfth or thirteenth century, that provides a system for acquiring knowledge of the seven liberal arts and other forms of learning through a programme of prayer, fasting, and contemplation of the notae — elaborate geometric and symbolic figures accompanied by sequences of divine names, Greek voces magicae, and Hebrew words, arranged into extended series of prayers (orationes). The practitioner is promised that diligent use of the system will result in divine infusion of the knowledge of grammar, rhetoric, dialectic, arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy, without the ordinary labour of study.

Structure and Use

The text exists in two main recensions: a shorter version and a longer version incorporating additional notae and prayers. The cycle of use for the complete system takes several months; intermediate cycles of shorter duration are also prescribed. The practitioner must observe strict conditions of ritual purity, undertake fasting and prayer at specified times, and contemplate the notae while reciting the associated prayers. The result is claimed to be not only the acquisition of encyclopedic knowledge but also prophetic dreams, visions of angels, and ultimately the direct perception of God.

Julien Véronèse's critical edition (L'Ars notoria au Moyen Âge: Introduction et édition critique, Sismel, 2007) is the scholarly standard. John of Morigny's Liber visionum (early fourteenth century), edited by Claire Fanger and Nicholas Watson (Penn State, 2015), is the most important medieval response to the Ars Notoria — a visionary revision of the system undertaken after Marian apparitions. Frank Klaassen's work situates the text within the broader manuscript tradition of English learned magic.

Theological Status

The Ars Notoria occupied an unusual theological position: it claimed to work through divine grace rather than demonic pact, making it arguably licit. Thomas Aquinas condemned it in the Summa theologiae (II-II, q. 96, a. 1) as vain (the system cannot achieve what it claims) and as implicitly involving demonic assistance (the voces magicae and geometric figures have no natural relationship to the knowledge they are supposed to infuse). Nevertheless, the text circulated widely in monastic and university contexts, and its practitioners evidently found the theological condemnation less than conclusive.

texts.title: Sworn Book of Honorius
texts.description: The Sworn Book of Honorius is a major medieval ritual magic text concerned with divine vision, angelic hierarchy, and ritual discipline.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Sworn Book of Honorius (Liber juratus Honorii) is a Latin magical text, probably composed in the thirteenth century, that presents itself as the surviving essence of a great magical library compiled by Honorius of Thebes and preserved only because ninety masters of magic swore to keep it secret and to pass it on to no more than three persons each. The framing narrative — the masters of magic assembling against papal persecution to preserve their knowledge — is itself significant as an early articulation of the magician's self-understanding as a persecuted keeper of ancient wisdom.

Contents

The Sworn Book is organized around a programme for achieving the beatific vision — the direct sight of God — through a course of prayer, fasting, and ritual practice extending over several months. The operative core is a set of prayers and conjurations for summoning the angel Hochmel (associated with divine wisdom), other celestial spirits, and eventually God himself. The text also includes procedures for more conventional magical ends: spirit conjuration for practical purposes, the construction of the Seal of God (a complex diagram combining divine names, astrological symbols, and angelic seals), and instructions for achieving invisibility.

Gösta Hedegård's critical edition (Liber iuratus Honorii: A Critical Edition of the Latin Version of the Sworn Book of Honorius, Almqvist and Wiksell, 2002) provides the scholarly text. Joseph Peterson's edition (Ibis Press, 2016) makes it available with English translation. The text occupies an interesting position between the Ars Notoria tradition (angelic infusion of knowledge through prayer and contemplation) and the demonic conjuration tradition (explicit spirit-binding for practical ends), and has been analysed by Kieckhefer, Klaassen, and Sophie Page in terms of this generic ambiguity.

texts.title: Forbidden Rites
texts.description: Richard Kieckhefer's Forbidden Rites edits and studies a fifteenth-century necromantic manual.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

Richard Kieckhefer's Forbidden Rites: A Necromancer's Manual of the Fifteenth Century (Penn State University Press, 1997) is both a critical edition and translation of the Munich Manual of demonic magic (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Clm 849) and a sustained scholarly analysis of what the text reveals about medieval learned magic and the social world in which it circulated. The Munich Manual is a Latin miscellany copied around the 1440s containing illusionist tricks, love magic using spirits, and full demonic conjuration rituals — the most complete surviving medieval Latin handbook of its kind.

The Text and Its Contents

Clm 849 contains three distinct types of material. The first section comprises "illusionist" experiments — procedures for creating apparent wonders (making a horse seem to have no head, making a banquet appear where none exists) that exploit psychological suggestion and natural properties rather than demonic power. The second section covers experiments involving spirit assistance for practical ends: finding hidden treasure, compelling love, causing discord, revealing thieves. The third section contains formal demonic conjuration: complete ritual procedures for summoning, binding, interrogating, and dismissing named demons.

Kieckhefer's edition provides the Latin text with facing English translation and extensive annotation identifying the demons named, the ritual sources, and the parallels in other magical manuscripts. His introductory chapters situate the text within the broader tradition of medieval Latin magic, discuss the question of how such a text was used (by whom, in what circumstances, with what expectations), and address the relationship between demonic conjuration and the theological concept of demonic pact.

Significance

The Munich Manual is significant as a primary document for the "clerical underworld" that Kieckhefer theorized in Magic in the Middle Ages: a text clearly designed for a literate, Latinately educated practitioner who expected to perform its rituals, not merely read about them. Its survival is partly accidental (it was bound with more respectable medical and astrological texts), and its content is more explicitly demonic than most surviving magical manuscripts — raising the question of what was destroyed that no longer survives. Forbidden Rites remains the model for how to approach a practical magic manuscript with scholarly rigour.

texts.title: The Transformations of Magic
texts.description: Frank Klaassen's study examines illicit learned magic in the later Middle Ages and Renaissance.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

Frank Klaassen's The Transformations of Magic: Illicit Learned Magic in the Later Middle Ages (Penn State University Press, 2013) is the most rigorous analysis of what Klaassen calls the "experiment literature" — the practical ritual magic books (nigromantic handbooks, ars notoria texts, Solomonic conjuration manuals) that circulated in manuscript among clerically trained readers in medieval England and Continental Europe from approximately 1300 to 1500. The book argues against two misleading models: the model that treats medieval magic as a unified, coherent tradition with stable content, and the model that treats the learned magical tradition as a pale copy of, or preparation for, Renaissance Hermeticism. Instead, Klaassen documents what actually survived in English manuscripts and shows how the content, purposes, and social contexts of learned magic shifted substantially over two centuries.

Argument and Evidence

Klaassen's central methodological contribution is the systematic survey of a defined corpus: he identifies and analyses approximately 270 surviving manuscripts containing ritual magic material in the medieval English tradition, rather than relying on a handful of well-known texts. This allows him to distinguish majority practice (ars notoria texts, image magic, simple conjurations) from exceptional cases (full demonic pact rituals), to trace the social circulation of texts across different manuscript contexts, and to identify two distinct types of transformation across the later medieval period.

The first transformation Klaassen identifies is a shift from "Solomonic" ritual magic — which emphasised the magician's moral purity, his Solomonic authority, and the coercive binding of spirits within a broadly Christian ritual framework — toward a more openly demonic conjuration literature in which the pact and explicit appeal to demonic power become more visible. The second transformation, running in the opposite direction, is the gradual absorption of Solomonic and image magic into the emerging idiom of "natural philosophy": Klaassen documents how later medieval readers and scribes increasingly framed magical operations in naturalistic terms, aligning them with Albertan and Arabist accounts of occult properties and celestial influence, effectively naturalising what earlier manuscripts had treated as operations of religious power.

Significance for Grimoire Studies

The book makes three major contributions to the study of the grimoire tradition. First, by documenting the manuscript evidence rather than relying on printed editions, Klaassen corrects the distortions introduced by the selective survival and editorial intervention of printed magical texts. Second, by demonstrating that "the learned magical tradition" is not a single thing but a set of practices and texts that changed substantially across two centuries, the book warns against the anachronistic projection of later Renaissance or early modern magical theory back onto medieval texts. Third, by focusing on what scribes and readers actually did with manuscripts — how they copied, excerpted, combined, and reorganised texts — Klaassen provides a model of manuscript-culture analysis that influenced subsequent work on the Ars Notoria, the Munich Manual, and Solomonic texts.

Context and Reception

Klaassen's work was preceded by and engages throughout with Richard Kieckhefer's Forbidden Rites (1997), which edited and analysed the Munich Manual of demonic magic, and with Claire Fanger's edited volumes on medieval ritual magic. It has been widely cited in subsequent scholarship on the grimoire tradition, including Dan Harms and Joseph Peterson's work on specific texts and Sophie Page's studies of magical manuscripts in institutional collections.

texts.title: Magic in the Cloister
texts.description: Sophie Page's monograph examines monastic and clerical engagements with occult approaches to the medieval universe.

texts.title: Invoking Angels
texts.description: Claire Fanger's edited collection studies theurgic ideas and practices from the thirteenth to sixteenth centuries.

texts.title: Unlocked Books
texts.description: Benedek Lang's study of manuscripts of learned magic in Central European libraries foregrounds codicology, ownership, and library context as evidence for learned magical transmission.

texts.title: Magic in Medieval Manuscripts
texts.description: Sophie Page's study examines medieval manuscript evidence for magical texts and the codicological contexts in which occult, devotional, and scientific materials circulated.

texts.title: Hazards of the Dark Arts
texts.description: Richard Kieckhefer's translation and study of Johannes Hartlieb's advice for princes places witchcraft, magic, and prohibited arts within fifteenth-century political and moral counsel.

texts.title: Liber Theysolius
texts.description: The Liber Theysolius is a medieval text associated in recent scholarship with wisdom, familiar spirits, and the pursuit of knowledge through ritualized contact.

texts.title: Liber Juratus Honorii
texts.description: The Liber Juratus Honorii, or Sworn Book of Honorius, is a major Latin ritual text concerning divine vision, angelic hierarchy, and sworn secrecy.

texts.title: Liber Razielis
texts.description: The Liber Razielis is a Latin textual complex associated with angelic revelation, astral knowledge, and the figure of Raziel.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Liber Razielis (Book of Raziel) is a Latin magical compendium, probably compiled in the thirteenth century, that draws heavily on Jewish sources — particularly the Hebrew Sepher Raziel ha-Malakh (Book of Raziel the Angel) — and on Arabic astrological magic. The Latin text presents itself as a revelation from the angel Raziel to Adam, transmitted through Enoch, Noah, Solomon, and ultimately to the practitioner. Its content includes angel magic, conjuration, astrological talismans, and a cosmological account of the seven heavens and their angelic inhabitants.

Sources and Transmission

The Liber Razielis is one of the most important texts for tracing the transmission of Jewish magical traditions into Latin learned magic. Its Hebrew source, the Sepher Raziel, is a complex compilation that was probably assembled in the thirteenth century but incorporates much older material, including traditions related to the Sepher ha-Razim and Geonic angel magic. The Latin translation transformed a Hebrew text structured around Jewish liturgical and cosmological categories into a form legible and usable within the framework of Latin clerical magic.

The text circulated in association with other Solomonic and angel magic texts — it appears in several manuscripts alongside the Clavicula Salomonis and the Ars Notoria — and was known to be one of the principal sources of Solomon's magical knowledge. David Pingree's work on the text and Gideon Bohak's analysis of the relationship between the Hebrew and Latin traditions provide the best scholarly guides to its transmission history.

texts.title: De radiis
texts.description: De radiis, associated with al-Kindi in Latin tradition, theorizes rays, celestial causality, and the efficacy of words and images in medieval natural philosophy.

texts.title: De imaginibus
texts.description: De imaginibus is a Latin astral-image text attributed to Thabit ibn Qurra and important for theories of talismanic images and celestial timing.

texts.title: Speculum astronomiae
texts.description: The Speculum astronomiae classifies astrological and image-making texts and became a crucial witness for scholastic attempts to distinguish licit astronomy from illicit image magic.

texts.title: A History of Magic and Experimental Science
texts.description: Lynn Thorndike's multi-volume history framed magic and experimental science as intertwined parts of medieval intellectual history, even where later scholarship has revised its assumptions.

texts.title: Clavicula Salomonis
texts.description: The Key of Solomon is a major Solomonic grimoire tradition transmitted in late medieval and early modern manuscripts, important for ritual purity, seals, conjurations, and textual instability.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Clavicula Salomonis (Key of Solomon) is the most widely circulated and extensively copied of the medieval and early modern Solomonic grimoires, surviving in over one hundred manuscripts in Latin, Italian, Hebrew, French, and English, ranging from the fourteenth century to the nineteenth. It is attributed to Solomon himself or to the transmission from Solomon to his son Roboam, and presents itself as a comprehensive practical manual for the conjuration of spirits, the construction of magical implements, and the performance of a wide range of ritual operations.

Structure and Contents

The text is typically organized in two books. Book I covers the practical ritual operations: how to conjure spirits to achieve specific ends (finding hidden treasures, obtaining love, causing invisibility, healing disease, inflicting harm). Book II covers the preparation of the magician and his instruments: the days and hours of the planets under which various operations should be conducted, the making and consecration of the magic circle, the pentacles attributed to the seven planets (each accompanied by a figure and a conjuration), the preparation of magical tools (knife, wand, lamen, robe, etc.), and the ritual of suffumigation and prayer.

The manuscript tradition is enormously complex. Joseph Peterson's online edition (Esoteric Archives) documents over fifty Latin and vernacular manuscripts; his printed edition (Weiser, 2004) provides the most thorough textual analysis available. S.L. Mathers's 1889 edition, based on British Museum manuscripts, was the first modern printed edition and shaped the occult revival's understanding of the text, though it combined several divergent manuscript families without adequate documentation.

Historical Development

The earliest datable manuscripts of the Clavicula Salomonis are from the fourteenth century; the text clearly assembled over a long period from multiple source traditions, incorporating elements of older Solomonic demonology, astrological image magic, and ritual prayer. The Hebrew Mafteah Shelomoh (Key of Solomon) tradition is related but may represent an independent development rather than a simple translation from Latin. The Arabic tradition of Solomonic conjuration (Solomon as Sulayman, master of jinn) provides a parallel context rather than a direct source. Frank Klaassen's work on the medieval English manuscript tradition and Pablo Torijano's on the ancient background remain the principal scholarly frameworks.

texts.title: Hygromanteia
texts.description: The Hygromanteia is a Byzantine Greek Solomonic ritual tradition that stands behind later Key of Solomon materials and complicates Latin-centered grimoire histories.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Hygromanteia (Greek: divination from water) is a Byzantine Greek astrological magic text, attributed to Solomon and surviving in several Greek manuscripts from the thirteenth century onward, though its compilation likely predates the surviving witnesses. The text is one of the principal Greek Solomonic texts and was a source for, or parallel development to, the Latin Clavicula Salomonis tradition. It combines astrological procedures, planetary images and talismans, and conjuration formulae within a Solomonic attribution framework.

Contents and Structure

The Hygromanteia addresses a wide range of practical magical procedures organized around the planets and their governing periods. Its contents include: procedures for using water, fire, and other substances for divination; instructions for making and using planetary images and talismans; formulas for conjuring planetary spirits; and procedures for a range of practical operations (finding hidden things, causing love, defeating enemies, obtaining favour from authorities). The attribution to Solomon and the invocation of divine and angelic names as authorizing forces situate it firmly within the Solomonic tradition.

Scholarship

Ioannis Marathakis's critical edition and English translation (The Magical Treatise of Solomon or Hygromanteia, Golden Hoard Press, 2011) made the text accessible to scholars working in the Latin and vernacular magical tradition. The edition establishes the manuscript tradition, provides the Greek text with English translation, and discusses the relationship of the Hygromanteia to the Latin Clavicula Salomonis — a relationship of partial correspondence and partial independence that suggests a shared tradition of Solomonic magic rather than simple textual derivation.

texts.title: Testament of Solomon
texts.description: The Testament of Solomon is a late antique demonological text that made Solomon a paradigmatic commander of spirits in later magical and literary traditions.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Testament of Solomon is a Greek pseudepigraphic text, probably composed between the first and fifth centuries CE, that narrates how King Solomon, aided by a magic ring given by the archangel Michael, summoned and interrogated demons, learning their names, their functions, the afflictions they cause, and the angels capable of thwarting them. The demons are then set to work constructing the Temple in Jerusalem. The text is the earliest systematic demonology in Greek and the foundational text of the Solomonic grimoire tradition: its framework of named demons bound to named angels, organized by Solomonic authority, provides the template replicated across two millennia of magical literature.

Structure and Contents

The narrative frame has Solomon receive a ring from Michael, inscribed with a pentagram, that gives him power over demons. He then successively summons thirty-six demons (later expanded in some manuscript traditions), each of whom reveals his name and the specific affliction he causes. Typical entries follow a pattern: the demon appears, reveals his name (often etymologized or pun-connected to his function), describes the diseases or misfortunes he inflicts, and reveals the angel whose name, written or spoken, can neutralize him. Some entries include planetary associations, gemstone affinities, and brief ritual instructions.

The text exists in several manuscript recensions of varying length and arrangement: McCown identified five principal recensions in his 1922 critical edition. The most important manuscripts are in the Bibliothèque nationale de France and the Vienna National Library. Dennis Duling's translation in Charlesworth's Old Testament Pseudepigrapha (Doubleday, 1983) is the standard English version.

Historical Significance

The Testament of Solomon is significant for several reasons. First, as a demonological text, it represents the earliest comprehensive name-catalogue of demons with individual attributes — a structure replicated in the Ars Goetia (part of the Lemegeton), the Book of Abramelin, and dozens of medieval and early modern grimoires. Second, as a pseudepigraphic text, it establishes the attribution strategy that would legitimise the entire subsequent Solomonic corpus: magical knowledge is Solomonic in origin, transmitted by divine gift (Michael's ring), and serves ultimately to build the Temple — that is, to serve God's purposes. Third, its composite nature — drawing on Jewish, Christian, pagan Greek, and possibly Egyptian elements — makes it evidence for the multicultural magical milieu of the late antique Mediterranean.

texts.title: Book of Oberon
texts.description: The Book of Oberon is an early modern English ritual magic compilation that preserves and transforms medieval Solomonic and spirit-conjuring materials.

texts.title: Book of Soyga
texts.description: The Book of Soyga is an early modern angelological and cryptographic ritual text associated with John Dee and earlier learned magical traditions.

texts.title: Heptameron
texts.description: The Heptameron is a ritual magic text attributed to Pietro d'Abano in print tradition and central to early modern angelic and planetary conjuration.

texts.title: Ars Almadel
texts.description: The Ars Almadel is a Solomonic angelic ritual text transmitted in early modern grimoire compilations and linked to older angelic invocation traditions.

texts.title: Ars Paulina
texts.description: The Ars Paulina is a Solomonic text of planetary and zodiacal angelic invocation preserved in early modern Lemegeton traditions.

texts.title: Ars Goetia
texts.description: The Ars Goetia is an early modern Solomonic demon catalogue and conjuring text whose roots and reception belong to the wider grimoire tradition.

texts.title: Lemegeton
texts.description: The Lemegeton or Lesser Key of Solomon is an early modern Solomonic compilation whose parts preserve angelic, demonic, and planetary ritual traditions.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Lemegeton (also called the Lesser Key of Solomon) is a compilation of five distinct magical texts, probably assembled in its current form in England in the seventeenth century, though each component text has earlier sources. The five parts are: the Ars Goetia (a catalogue of seventy-two demons with their seals and powers); the Ars Theurgia-Goetia (spirits of the cardinal and intermediate directions); the Ars Paulina (planetary angels of the hours); the Ars Almadel (angels of the four altitudes); and the Ars Notoria (a memory and wisdom system using prayer and divine names). The compilation circulated extensively in seventeenth-century English manuscript culture — surviving in dozens of copies — before its first modern printed edition by Mathers and Crowley in 1904.

The Ars Goetia

The most influential component is the Ars Goetia, which catalogues seventy-two demons in the tradition of the Testament of Solomon: each demon is given a name, rank (king, duke, marquis, count, etc.), seal, number of legions commanded, and special powers (knowledge of arts and sciences, revealing hidden things, building structures, inciting love or discord, etc.). The catalogue derives from earlier sources — particularly the Pseudomonarchia Daemonum appended to Johann Weyer's De praestigiis daemonum (1563) — and represents a systematic elaboration of the Solomonic spirit catalogue tradition. Joseph Peterson's 2001 edition of the complete Lemegeton is the standard scholarly resource, documenting the manuscript sources and their relationships.

The Ars Notoria

The Ars Notoria (Notory Art) is the oldest component and the most distinct in character: rather than conjuring demons, it seeks knowledge and wisdom through a system of prayer, meditation, and contemplation of divine words and figures (notae). The text claims that by meditating on the notae and reciting the associated prayers over a period of weeks, the practitioner will acquire the seven liberal arts and other forms of knowledge infused by divine grace. This tradition, which emphasizes the practitioner's religious purity and the angelic mediation of knowledge, is analyzed in detail by Claire Fanger and Nicholas Watson in their editions of John of Morigny's Liber visionum (a related text) and by Julien Véronèse in his critical edition of the Notory Art.

texts.title: Grimorium Verum
texts.description: Grimorium Verum is an early modern printed grimoire important for the post-medieval reception and reorganization of spirit conjuration traditions.

texts.title: Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses
texts.description: The Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses are early modern/modern grimoire traditions relevant to the long reception of biblical magical authority.

texts.title: Liber Lunae
texts.description: The Liber Lunae is a Latin lunar and astral ritual text associated with image magic, timing, and the broader learned magical manuscript corpus.

texts.title: De occultis operibus naturae
texts.description: De occultis operibus naturae names a scholastic problem field concerning hidden natural powers, occult properties, and the boundary between nature and magic.

texts.title: Secretum Secretorum

texts.title: Opus Majus
texts.description: Roger Bacon's Opus Majus is central to medieval discussions of experiment, language, optics, astrology, and the status of knowledge later associated with magic and science.

texts.title: De universo
texts.description: William of Auvergne's De universo is central to theological discussion of spirits, demons, image magic, and the created order.

texts.title: Etymologiae
texts.description: Isidore of Seville's Etymologiae transmitted influential classifications of magic, divination, and pagan learning to medieval encyclopedic culture.

texts.title: De mineralibus
texts.description: Albertus Magnus's De mineralibus is important for scholastic discussion of stones, occult properties, natural powers, and lapidary traditions.

texts.title: De divinatione daemonum
texts.description: Augustine's De divinatione daemonum helped shape Christian explanations of divination, demons, signs, and illicit curiosity.

texts.title: Liber experimentorum
texts.description: Liber experimentorum names a family or genre of experiment-books in medieval learned magic, where recipes, trials, secrets, and operations circulate as textual experiments rather than stable authored treatises.

texts.title: Buch aller verbotenen Kunst
texts.description: Johannes Hartlieb's Buch aller verbotenen Kunst, or Book of All Forbidden Arts, is a fifteenth-century German treatment of prohibited arts, witchcraft, and magical practices for princely and moral instruction.

texts.title: De Occulta Philosophia
texts.description: The most comprehensive Renaissance synthesis of occult philosophy, completed in manuscript c.1510 by Cornelius Agrippa and published in Cologne 1531-1533. Three books treat natural magic (book I), celestial and mathematical magic (book II), and ceremonial magic including spirit conjuration (book III). Agrippa drew on Ficino, Pico, Trithemius, and extensively on medieval learned magic manuscripts. Frank Klaassen has shown that book III is substantially continuous with the Munich Manual, the Sworn Book of Honorius, and other late medieval necromantic texts, directly undermining the sharp medieval-Renaissance break posited by Yates. The work was enormously influential on subsequent learned magic including Dee's Elizabethan practice.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

De occulta philosophia libri tres (Three Books of Occult Philosophy) by Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim was first circulated in manuscript from around 1510, circulated widely in that form through networks connecting the Rhine valley humanists to Italian Neoplatonists, and finally published in printed form in 1531 (Cologne, Johannes Soter). A heavily revised version appeared the same year in Antwerp. The work is the most ambitious encyclopedic synthesis of Renaissance occult philosophy: a three-book structure corresponding to the three worlds of Neoplatonic cosmology — the elemental world, the celestial world, and the intellectual world — and providing a comprehensive account of the theory and practice of natural, celestial, and ceremonial magic.

Structure and Contents

Book I (Natural Magic) covers the occult properties of the four elements, the sympathies and antipathies among things in the elemental world, the medical and magical uses of plants, stones, and metals, the doctrine of occult qualities (following pseudo-Albertus and al-Kindi), the role of the imagination and passions in magical operations, and the theory of the world-soul as the mediating principle through which magical influence travels.

Book II (Celestial or Mathematical Magic) addresses the seven planets and their influence on temperament and character, the construction of astrological talismans and magical images, the magical squares (camea) attributed to each planet (with their numerological and geometric properties), the magical significance of numbers, proportions, and geometric figures, and the doctrine of the fixed stars and their images.

Book III (Ceremonial or Divine Magic) is the most contentious and the most theologically ambitious. It treats the angelic and demonic hierarchies in their relationship to the divine names; the Kabbalah as a technology of divine name manipulation; the power of words, letters, characters, and seals; and the operations by which the magus might ascend through the celestial hierarchy to communicate with angels, culminating in the figure of the homo divinus who unites the three worlds in a single act of mystical gnosis. This book draws heavily on Pico della Mirandola, Reuchlin's Kabbalistic works, and Trithemius.

Sources and Method

The erudition deployed across the three books is remarkable. Agrippa synthesizes Ficino's De vita and Platonic Theology, Pico's Conclusiones, the pseudo-Albertian natural magic treatises, al-Kindi's De radiis, the Picatrix, Proclus, Iamblichus, the Corpus Hermeticum, Pseudo-Dionysius, the Sefer Yetzirah, and hundreds of other sources from ancient, Arabic, Jewish, and Christian traditions. The organization is not merely encyclopedic but argumentative: Agrippa wants to demonstrate that all these traditions converge on a unified account of how occult power operates in the universe, and that a properly trained philosophical magician can work within this system without demonic pact.

Manuscript Tradition and Printed Editions

The manuscript versions of De occulta philosophia circulated from 1510 onward, with a copy sent to Trithemius (who responded cautiously but approvingly) and others reaching Erasmus's circle. The differences between the manuscript versions and the 1531 printed text are significant: Agrippa removed some of the more provocative material on ceremonial magic and added a preface emphasizing the work's natural-philosophical orientation. The 1531 Antwerp edition incorporates further revisions. The 1651 English edition (attributed to J.F.) is the version most familiar to Anglophone occultists but contains numerous translation errors and was accompanied by the spurious Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy, which has caused confusion about the limits of Agrippa's authorship.

Scholarly Reception

Charles Nauert's Agrippa and the Crisis of Renaissance Thought (1965) remains the standard scholarly biography and remains essential for understanding the De occulta philosophia in context. Brian Copenhaver's work on Renaissance magic has repeatedly returned to Agrippa as a central case study in the relationship between Neoplatonic philosophy and practical magic. Wouter Hanegraaff's Esotericism and the Academy (2012) treats the work as a founding text in the Western esoteric tradition. For the manuscript tradition, see the studies of V. Perrone Compagni, who produced the critical edition (Brill, 1992).

texts.title: Steganographia
texts.title_original: Steganographia hoc est ars per occultam scripturam animi sui voluntatem absentibus aperiendi certa
texts.description: Written c.1499 by Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, and circulated in manuscript for over a century before print publication in Frankfurt (1606). Books I and II describe a system of angel magic for long-distance communication through angelic intermediaries, firmly within late medieval spirit magic traditions. Book III was demonstrated in 1998 by Thomas Ernst to conceal cryptographic ciphers beneath the apparent magical text. Placed on the Index Librorum Prohibitorum in 1609 and removed in 1900, the Steganographia influenced Agrippa's angelic cosmology, fascinated John Dee, and contributed to early modern debates about the boundary between natural and demonic magic.

texts.title: Corpus Hermeticum (Ficino Translation)
texts.title_original: Pimander seu de potestate et sapientia divina
texts.description: Marsilio Ficino's Latin translation of the fourteen Greek texts known as the Corpus Hermeticum, completed in 1463 at the direction of Cosimo de' Medici before Ficino had finished his Plato translations. Published as Pimander in 1471 (Treviso). The Hermetic texts, then believed to preserve ancient Egyptian wisdom older than Plato and Moses (a dating demolished by Isaac Casaubon in 1614), provided Ficino and his circle with what they took to be a prisca theologia supporting natural magic and Neoplatonist cosmology. Frances Yates's thesis that Hermeticism drove the Renaissance scientific revolution depended heavily on the influence of this translation.

texts.title: De Vita Coelitus Comparanda
texts.title_original: De vita libri tres, liber tertius
texts.description: The third book of Ficino's De Vita (1489), treating how to attract stellar influences through talismans, music, scents, foods, and sympathetic correspondence. The text draws on the Picatrix, Pseudo-Ptolemy's De imaginibus, and the pseudo-Hermetic De quindecim stellis, combining astral medicine with a Neoplatonist theory of spiritus mediation. Klaassen has argued that the text has extensive commonalities with medieval ritual magic and was used as a source by sixteenth-century ritual magic practitioners. D.P. Walker's Spiritual and Demonic Magic (1958) remains the standard scholarly treatment, arguing that Ficino attempted to limit his magic to the spiritus level, avoiding demonic invocation.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

De vita coelitus comparanda (On Drawing Life from the Sky), the third and most controversial book of Marsilio Ficino's De vita trilogy, was completed and published in 1489 under Medici patronage in Florence. Books I and II of the trilogy address the health of the scholar (prone to Saturnine melancholy) and the prolongation of life; Book III proposes a system of astral medicine and magic by which the scholar-philosopher can mitigate the cold and dryness of Saturnine influence by attracting solar and Jovian spiritus through material and ritual means. It is the founding text of Renaissance natural magic as a philosophical discipline.

The Argument

Ficino's argument rests on three connected Neoplatonic claims. First, the cosmos is pervaded by a subtle spiritus mundi — a vital, pneumatic medium analogous to the spirit of the individual human body — through which celestial influences flow into terrestrial things. Second, things in the sublunary world are related to each other and to the celestial bodies through bonds of sympathy (likeness attracts like) and antipathy, so that specific plants, stones, metals, foods, colours, and sounds resonate with specific planetary influences. Third, the human spirit, as the nexus between body and soul, is especially susceptible to these influences and can be deliberately charged or depleted of specific planetary spiritus through exposure to the appropriate material and sensory environment.

The therapeutic application: a scholar of melancholic temperament is dominated by Saturn — planet of cold, dryness, contemplation, and solitude. Saturnine excess produces depression, physical debility, and intellectual rigidity. By deliberately surrounding himself with solar and Jovian materials — gold, amber, saffron, warm foods, cheerful music in the Dorian mode, sunlight, and the company of kind friends — the scholar attracts solar and Jovian spiritus, counteracting Saturnine excess and restoring the pneumatic balance necessary for healthy contemplation.

The Philosophical Problem

The problem, identified by D.P. Walker in his foundational analysis, is that Ficino's theoretical apparatus derives from Neoplatonic sources — above all Iamblichus and Proclus — that were not entirely free of demonic implication. The theurgic operations these philosophers described operated through daemons as well as through impersonal sympathies; Proclus's account of the sympathy between like and like shaded into a world populated by spiritual agents responsive to the magician's calls. Ficino insisted, in the self-defensive preface he added to later editions, that his magic operated through purely natural causes; whether this insulation was philosophically coherent or merely prudential remains an open question.

texts.title: Oration on the Dignity of Man
texts.description: Prefatory oration by Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, written c.1486 as an introduction to his 900 Theses (Conclusiones), a university disputation that Pope Innocent VIII ultimately condemned. Pico presents humanity as uniquely capable of ascending through all orders of being, and presents magic alongside Kabbalah as a demonstrative natural science. The Oration distinguishes magia naturalis, which operates through natural sympathies and is licit, from goetia, which employs demons and is condemned. Published posthumously. Frances Yates treated it as the founding document of a Renaissance Hermetic-magical worldview; subsequent scholars have offered more qualified readings.

texts.title: Monas Hieroglyphica
texts.description: A short cryptic treatise by John Dee, published in Antwerp in 1564 and dedicated to Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian II. Organized around an alchemical-astronomical-magical symbol Dee called the monad, the text claims to derive a unified symbolic language from planetary, elemental, zodiacal, and Kabbalistic correspondences. Dee considered it among his most important theoretical works. The Monas has been variously interpreted as alchemical treatise, Kabbalistic commentary, and purely mathematical symbolism. Nicholas Clulee's study John Dee's Natural Philosophy (1988) remains the standard scholarly treatment of Dee's mathematical and occult theories.

texts.title: Mysteriorum Libri Quinque
texts.description: John Dee's record of the first five of his angelic conferences with scryers including Bartholomew Hickman and primarily Edward Kelley, conducted from 1583 onward. The manuscripts, preserved in the British Library and published in critical edition by Joseph Peterson (2003), document the procedures, visions, angelic speeches, and tables of correspondences that constitute the Enochian system. Frank Klaassen has argued that the angel operations in these records are firmly within the tradition of late medieval angelic conjuration rather than a new Hermetic or Neoplatonist departure; the form of the conferences directly parallels procedures in the Sworn Book of Honorius and Ars Notoria.

texts.title: Magia Naturalis
texts.title_original: Magia naturalis sive de miraculis rerum naturalium
texts.description: Compiled by Giovanni Battista della Porta of Naples. First edition 1558, expanded from four books to twenty books in the 1589 edition. Della Porta systematized a natural philosophy of sympathies, antipathies, and occult properties, incorporating phenomena from alchemy, gardening, optics, distillation, magnetism, and cosmetics alongside traditional magical procedures. The expanded 1589 edition was widely translated and circulated throughout Europe. It represents the late Renaissance attempt to naturalize the content of medieval magic by framing it within an Aristotelian natural philosophy of hidden properties. The Accademia dei Segreti founded by della Porta was the first learned society focused on natural experiment.

texts.title: Arbatel de Magia Veterum
texts.description: Latin grimoire of unknown authorship printed at Basel in 1575, purporting to be the first of nine books of Olympic spirit magic. Only one book survives in print. The Arbatel presents a system of seven Olympic spirits governing planetary spheres, accessible through prayer and ethical preparation rather than through elaborate demonic conjuration. Its tone is markedly more devotional and Protestant-inflected than most grimoires of the period. Klaassen notes that editions of the Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy, the Arbatel, and related texts were printed around the same time, suggesting a market for printed ceremonial magic. Joseph Peterson produced the standard modern critical edition.

texts.title: Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy
texts.description: A Latin grimoire of spirit conjuration printed under Agrippa's name from 1559 onward, though likely not by Agrippa. Klaassen identifies three editions in the mid-sixteenth century and notes it was bound with the Arbatel. The text concerns the conjuration of spirits using circles, pentacles, and Solomonic procedures, drawing on and extending the tradition of late medieval demonic magic rather than the philosophical natural magic of Agrippa's genuine De Occulta Philosophia. Its circulation under Agrippa's authority demonstrates the tendency of sixteenth-century grimoire compilers to attach their texts to prestigious Renaissance names, conflating the philosophical and the practical registers of occult writing.

texts.title: Polygraphia
texts.description: Printed posthumously in 1518 with a full title indicating its dedication to Emperor Maximilian, Polygraphia was the first printed book on cryptography and the first of Trithemius's works to reach print. It presents a system of letter-substitution ciphers and encoded alphabets without the angelic or magical framing of Steganographia. Its publication established Trithemius's reputation as a pioneer of cryptography separate from his reputation as a magician. The relationship between Polygraphia and Steganographia has been illuminated by modern cryptographers who demonstrated that Steganographia's Book III conceals legitimate ciphers beneath magical apparatus, while Polygraphia presents the ciphers transparently.

texts.title: The Discoverie of Witchcraft
texts.description: Published in London in 1584 by Reginald Scot, a Kentish gentleman. The most systematic English-language skeptical critique of witch-hunting in the sixteenth century, arguing that witchcraft accusations rest on fraud, delusion, poverty, and clerical manipulation, and that demonic operations are physically impossible. The Discoverie also contains extensive appendices on practical magic, conjuring tricks, and Solomonic procedures, making it an inadvertent sourcebook for later grimoire compilers. Klaassen notes that Scot's book was reissued in the seventeenth century by publishers who recognized its commercial value to magical practitioners. King James I reportedly ordered copies burned, though this claim is difficult to verify.

texts.title: De Praestigiis Daemonum
texts.title_original: De praestigiis daemonum et incantationibus ac veneficiis
texts.description: Published at Basel in 1563 by Johann Weyer, physician to Duke William of Jülich-Cleves-Berg. Weyer argued that confessions of witchcraft reflect delusion and melancholy rather than genuine demonic pacts, and that old women accused as witches lacked the capacity for real commerce with demons. He accepted the existence of powerful demons while denying effective human magic, a position developed from his teacher Agrippa. The work underwent six Latin editions and several vernacular translations in the later sixteenth century and was a major reference for skeptical thinkers including Reginald Scot. Bodin attacked it vigorously in De la Démonomanie (1580).

texts.title: Spiritual and Demonic Magic: From Ficino to Campanella
texts.description: Published by D.P. Walker at the Warburg Institute in 1958. The first systematic scholarly account of Renaissance magic's relationship to Neoplatonism, demonology, and natural philosophy. Walker distinguished spiritual magic, operating through the pneuma or spiritus mediating between soul and body, from demonic magic involving explicit summons of evil spirits. He demonstrated that Ficino's De Vita Coelitus Comparanda was genuinely a magical text, not merely philosophical metaphor, while arguing Ficino sought to remain on the natural side of the spiritual-demonic boundary. Walker's framework preceded and shaped Frances Yates's broader Hermetic thesis. The book covers Ficino, Pico, Pomponazzi, Agrippa, Cardano, della Porta, Bruno, and Campanella.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

D.P. Walker's Spiritual and Demonic Magic from Ficino to Campanella, first published by the Warburg Institute in 1958 (and reissued in paperback by Penn State University Press, 2000), is the foundational scholarly study of Renaissance learned magic as a philosophical problem. Written before Frances Yates's more ambitious synthetic works, the book is more cautious in its causal claims and more attentive to the philosophical difficulties confronting Renaissance thinkers who sought to claim legitimate natural-philosophical authority for operations that resembled, and often derived from, the demonic magic condemned by medieval theologians. It remains required reading for any study of Renaissance occult philosophy.

Argument

Walker's central question is: how did Renaissance Neoplatonist magicians — above all Ficino and his successors — attempt to distinguish their operations from demonic magic, and how successful were these attempts philosophically and practically? The problem Walker identifies is structural: the theoretical framework through which Ficino explained the efficacy of his astral magic (the doctrine of the world-soul, pneumatic mediation, the sympathy of like for like) derived from Neoplatonic sources — Plotinus, Iamblichus, Proclus — that were not themselves entirely innocent of demonic implication. Iamblichus and Proclus had both discussed the role of daemons in ritual operations; the intermediary spirits of Neoplatonic theurgy shaded imperceptibly into the Christian demons that any orthodox theologian was required to condemn.

Walker traces the problem through a sequence of case studies: Ficino's De vita coelitus comparanda, Pico della Mirandola's attempt to distinguish Kabbalah from demonic magic, Francesco Giorgi's Harmonia mundi, Cornelius Agrippa's De occulta philosophia, Giambattista della Porta's Magia naturalis, the music-magic theory of Ficino's successors, and the later career of the tradition through Francesco Patrizi, Giordano Bruno, and Tommaso Campanella. In each case, Walker shows both the sophistication of the attempt to naturalize magical operations and the points at which the naturalization broke down — where the philosopher needed to invoke spirit-working that could not be fully distinguished from demonic cooperation.

Key Concepts

"Spiritual magic" in Walker's usage designates operations that work through the spiritus — the subtle pneumatic vehicle of the soul and the world-soul — and that their practitioners claimed were purely natural, operating through the sympathetic relationships between celestial and terrestrial things. "Demonic magic" designates operations that require explicit cooperation with demonic or angelic intelligences as rational, personal agents. Walker's argument is that the boundary between these two types was genuinely contested and philosophically unstable throughout the tradition he surveys.

Walker also contributed the concept of "spiritual magic as a problem of orthodoxy" — the observation that Renaissance philosophers were not simply operating in a pre-scientific context where magic was unproblematically acceptable, but were themselves aware of the theological dangers and sought to manage them. This insight corrected older historiography that presented Renaissance magic as naive belief, and anticipated more recent work on learned magic as a theoretically sophisticated practice.

Legacy

Walker's book was the immediate predecessor and in some respects the model for Frances Yates's work, and the relationship between them is worth noting. Walker's caution and his focus on philosophical tensions contrasts with Yates's synthetic ambition; scholars who found Yates's thesis too sweeping have generally returned to Walker's more cautious framework. Brian Copenhaver's philosophical analysis of Ficino builds directly on Walker; D.P. Walker's other work on music and magic (in essays collected in Music, Spirit and Language in the Renaissance, ed. Pennelope Gouk, 1985) extends the book's concerns. The Walker tradition — careful philosophical reading, attention to the natural/demonic distinction, sensitivity to the risks faced by Renaissance magical thinkers — remains the dominant approach in the field.

texts.title: Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition
texts.description: Published by Frances Yates at the University of Chicago Press in 1964. The founding text of what scholars call the Yates thesis: that Hermeticism and natural magic were central to Renaissance culture, that Ficino and Pico inaugurated a new Hermetic-magical worldview, and that this tradition, carried by Bruno, Dee, and others, contributed to the Scientific Revolution. Yates drew on Walker and on the Warburg tradition of iconological analysis. The thesis was challenged by Brian Vickers, Brian Copenhaver, and most recently Frank Klaassen, who argued that Renaissance ritual magic was continuous with medieval practice rather than the sanitized Hermetic-natural magic Yates envisioned. The book remains a landmark of historiography despite these revisions.

texts.title: The Occult Philosophy in the Elizabethan Age
texts.description: Frances Yates's last major book, published by Routledge in 1979, extending her Hermetic thesis to Elizabethan England through the figures of John Dee, Christopher Marlowe's Doctor Faustus, Edmund Spenser, and Philip Sidney. Yates argued that a Kabbalist-Hermetic magical philosophy, transmitted through Agrippa and Dee, shaped Elizabethan literature and intellectual culture. The book's treatment of Dee as a Hermetic philosopher in the Ficino-Pico tradition was challenged by Klaassen, whose study of Dee's magical manuscripts showed his practice rooted in medieval ritual traditions rather than Hermetic natural magic. Yates's reading of Spenser and Marlowe has proved more durable than her account of Dee's specific practices.

texts.title: Grimoires: A History of Magic Books
texts.description: Published by Owen Davies at Oxford University Press in 2009. The most comprehensive survey of grimoire history from ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt through the twenty-first century, covering medieval manuscript circulation, the impact of the printing press on grimoire diffusion, the French popular grimoire tradition (Grand Albert, Petit Albert, Dragon Rouge), nineteenth-century occultist editions (Mathers, Waite, Levi), and contemporary global usage. Davies situates the grimoire tradition in social history, examining who owned, copied, sold, and used magical books across different social strata. The book is essential reading for understanding the gap between manuscript-based learned magic and the popular print tradition that emerged after 1500.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

Owen Davies's Grimoires: A History of Magic Books (Oxford University Press, 2009) is the most comprehensive historical survey of the grimoire as a genre from antiquity to the present and the essential starting point for any study of the magical book as a cultural artefact. The book traces the transformation of learned magical manuscripts into commercial publications, following the grimoire through the hand-press era, the chapbook revolution of the eighteenth century, the Victorian occult revival, the twentieth-century paperback market, and finally the digital age.

Argument and Structure

Davies's central argument is that the grimoire is not a timeless repository of esoteric knowledge but a historically conditioned object that changes with its means of production, its social context, and its intended audience. The ancient and medieval manuscript grimoire (expensive, restricted, circulating among literate elites) differs fundamentally from the eighteenth-century French chapbook grimoire (Grand Albert, Petit Albert, Dragon Rouge), which was designed for a literate popular market. The nineteenth-century occult revival editions of Mathers and Waite imposed scholarly apparatus and ritual significance on texts that had long circulated as practical handbooks. The twentieth-century paperback grimoire (Llewellyn, Weiser) addresses a self-identified magical community with different needs and assumptions.

The book's chapters proceed chronologically and by geography: ancient Mesopotamian and Egyptian magical books; Jewish and Christian late antique texts; medieval European manuscripts; the Arabic and Mediterranean traditions; the early modern print era; the French chapbook tradition; American popular magic (hoodoo, Pennsylvania Dutch hex); the Victorian occult revival; and twentieth-century print and digital magic. Each chapter combines primary-source analysis with attention to the social history of production, circulation, and use.

Significance

Davies's book is particularly important for two contributions. First, it documents the role of popular print culture — the chapbook, the pamphlet, the cheap pamphlet grimoire — in transmitting magical tradition to social strata far below the learned clerical elite that had been the focus of most previous grimoire scholarship. Second, it demonstrates the global reach of the grimoire tradition, including its transmission to colonial and post-colonial contexts in Africa, the Caribbean, and North America, where texts like the Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses entered African-American hoodoo practice.

texts.title: The Book of Oberon
texts.description: Critical transcription and annotated translation of Folger Shakespeare Library MS Vb.26, a late sixteenth-century English manuscript of approximately 450 pages. Edited by Daniel Harms, James R. Clark, and Joseph H. Peterson, published by Llewellyn in 2015. The manuscript combines Solomonic spirit lists drawn from Agrippa and related sources with vernacular fairy magic, conjuring for treasure and love, and practical operations in both Latin and English. The edition exemplifies how the Elizabethan period combined learned Continental magic traditions with native English vernacular practices. Klaassen's Making Magic in Elizabethan England examined related manuscripts from the same period.

texts.title: Making Magic in Elizabethan England
texts.title_original: Making Magic in Elizabethan England: Two Early Modern Vernacular Books of Magic
texts.description: Edited volume published by Frank Klaassen at Penn State University Press (2019), providing critical editions and analysis of two Elizabethan vernacular magic manuscripts. The volume demonstrates how early modern English practitioners engaged with Continental learned magic traditions including Agrippa, Dee, and earlier Solomonic texts while producing vernacular adaptations that combined learned and popular elements. Klaassen situates these manuscripts within his broader argument about the continuity of medieval ritual magic into the early modern period, showing that sixteenth-century English practitioners drew on the same core of medieval spirit-conjuring texts as their fifteenth-century predecessors, supplemented by printed Renaissance sources.

texts.title: The Magic of Rogues
texts.description: Published by Frank Klaassen and Sharon Hubbs Wright at Penn State University Press (2021) in the Magic in History Sourcebooks series. Examines legal documents and magic texts from two early Tudor cases where English authorities confronted practicing magicians, exploring how practitioners thought about the world, where they obtained their ideas, and how their magic was supposed to work. The volume provides critical editions of the relevant manuscripts and legal records alongside analysis of the practices involved. Demonstrates the vitality of the medieval necromantic tradition in early sixteenth-century England and the social networks through which magical manuscripts circulated among clerics, practitioners, and curious laypeople.

texts.title: The Magus
texts.description: Compiled by Francis Barrett and published in London in 1801. A substantial compilation drawing heavily on Agrippa's De Occulta Philosophia, Robert Turner's seventeenth-century English translations of magical texts, and related Renaissance and medieval sources. The Magus marks the transition from manuscript and early print circulation of learned magic to Romantic-era popular occultism. Barrett organized his compilation in three parts: natural magic, magnetism and alchemy, and ritual and talismanic magic. The Magus served as a conduit bringing Agrippa's framework and associated Renaissance material to nineteenth-century English-language audiences and influenced later figures including Edward Bulwer-Lytton and Eliphas Lévi.

texts.title: Sepher ha-Razim
texts.description: The Book of Mysteries (Sepher ha-Razim) is a Hebrew magical handbook whose compilation is usually dated to the 7th–10th century CE, though it draws on much older traditions of angel magic. Attributed to Noah and transmitted through Shem, the text organizes the seven heavens and their angelic inhabitants, providing adjurations, incantations, and ritual procedures keyed to each heavenly realm. Its framework of named angels ordered by celestial sphere connects to both the Solomonic grimoire tradition and broader Jewish mystical cosmology. The standard critical edition is Mordecai Margalioth's 1966 Hebrew text; Morgan's English translation appeared in 1983.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Sepher ha-Razim (Book of Mysteries) is a Hebrew magical handbook whose compilation is usually dated to the Geonic period (sixth to tenth centuries CE), though it draws on material that is almost certainly earlier — some scholars detect traditions going back to the Second Temple period. It is attributed to Noah, who received it from the angel Raziel, transmitted it through Shem, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, and ultimately Solomon, who used it in the construction of the Temple. This chain of transmission connects the text to the Solomonic authority framework while locating its ultimate origin in antediluvian divine revelation.

Structure and Contents

The text is organized around the seven heavens, each presided over by a named angelic prince and populated by named angelic servants whose functions and the periods of their activity are specified. For each heavenly realm, the text provides: the names of the ruling angel and his subordinates, the days and hours of their activity, adjurations invoking them, and specific practical procedures (prescriptions for achieving various ends through the proper invocation of the appropriate heaven's angels). Operations range from healing and protection through love magic, invisibility, and the harming of enemies.

The standard critical edition is Mordecai Margalioth's 1966 Hebrew text. Michael Morgan's English translation (Scholars Press, 1983) made the text accessible to non-Hebrew readers and remains the standard English version. The text is a key document for the history of Jewish magical practice and provides essential context for understanding the relationship between Jewish angel magic and the Latin and Greek Solomonic tradition.

Significance

The Sepher ha-Razim is significant for several reasons. Its hierarchical organization of named angels by heavenly sphere anticipates the spirit catalogues of the medieval Solomonic grimoires. Its adjuration formulas — commands addressed to named spirits invoking God's authority — provide the direct precedent for the Latin conjuration literature. Its attribution to Noah and Raziel rather than Solomon marks a distinct tradition of antediluvian revealed magic that parallels the Solomonic tradition without being identical to it. Gideon Bohak's Ancient Jewish Magic (2008) situates it within the wider context of Jewish magical practice.

texts.title: Solomon the Esoteric King
texts.description: Pablo Torijano's Solomon the Esoteric King: From King to Magus, Development of a Tradition (Brill, 2002) traces the transformation of the biblical Solomon into a master of demons, occult knowledge, and magical authority across Jewish, Christian, and Islamic sources from the Second Temple period through the medieval era. Torijano analyzes the Testament of Solomon, Solomonic adjurations, and the pseudepigraphic authority of the Solomonic corpus as a cross-cultural phenomenon. Reviewed by Frank Klaassen and others as foundational for understanding Solomonic attribution as a legitimating strategy.

texts.title: Ancient Jewish Magic: A History
texts.description: Gideon Bohak's Ancient Jewish Magic: A History (Cambridge University Press, 2008) surveys Jewish magical practice from the biblical period through the end of antiquity, drawing on amulets, magical papyri, incantation bowls, genizah fragments, and rabbinic literature. The book argues that Jewish magic was a coherent and distinctive tradition with identifiable practices, texts, and practitioners, and that it contributed substantially to the broader Mediterranean magical culture from which Christian and Islamic magical traditions emerged. Essential for the pre-history of the Solomonic grimoire corpus.

texts.title: Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, Volume 1
texts.description: James H. Charlesworth's Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, Volume 1 (Doubleday, 1983) contains Dennis Duling's annotated English translation of the Testament of Solomon, with introduction covering date, provenance, original language (Greek), manuscript tradition, and theological significance. The volume remains the standard reference collection for pseudepigraphic literature adjacent to the Hebrew Bible and New Testament, placing Solomonic demonology within the context of Jewish apocalyptic and early Christian writing.

texts.title: Mafteah Shelomoh
texts.description: The Mafteah Shelomoh (Key of Solomon in Hebrew) survives in several medieval and early modern manuscripts, of which the most significant for scholarship is British Museum MS Oriental 14759, edited by Herman Gollancz in 1914. The Hebrew recension of the Clavicula Salomonis tradition shows independence from the Latin manuscript families while sharing ritual categories including conjurations, pentacles, and spirit hierarchies attributed to Solomon. Its relationship to the Latin Clavicula Salomonis remains debated: whether the Hebrew text preceded or derived from Latin versions is a key question in Solomonic textual scholarship.

texts.title: Summa theologiae
texts.description: Thomas Aquinas's Summa theologiae (c. 1265–1274), composed at Paris, Naples, and Rome, contains the most systematic scholastic treatment of divination, astrology, demonic magic, and the limits of natural philosophy in medieval Latin thought. Questions in the Secunda secundae (ST II-II, qq. 92–96) address superstition, divination, and the pact with demons; earlier sections treat angels and demons as rational creatures with limited but real causal powers. Aquinas's framework dominated university theology through the fifteenth century and informed every major scholastic classification of magic.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Summa theologiae of Thomas Aquinas, composed between approximately 1265 and 1274 at Paris, Naples, and Rome (left incomplete at his death in 1274), is the most systematic and authoritative synthesis of medieval scholastic theology and the work that dominated Catholic theological education from the fourteenth century through the Second Vatican Council. For the history of magic, two sections are of primary importance: the treatment of angels and demons in the Prima Pars (qq. 50–64, 106–114) and the discussion of superstition, divination, and forbidden arts in the Secunda secundae (qq. 92–96).

Angels, Demons, and Causal Powers

In the Prima Pars, Aquinas treats angels as pure intellectual substances, created good by God, some of whom fell through pride — the demons. As intellectual substances, both angels and demons have real causal powers: they can move bodies, affect the imagination and senses, influence the passions, and produce what appear to be marvellous effects through their superior knowledge of natural causes and their capacity to move matter more rapidly than human agents. However, they cannot override free will (because the will is moved only by the intellect and by God), and they cannot perform genuine miracles (which are reserved to God alone). The demonic wonders described in scripture are either real natural effects produced through superior knowledge, or illusions (praestigia) affecting only the senses or imagination.

This framework — demons as real agents with limited natural powers — was not merely theological but had direct practical implications for how inquisitors, theologians, and natural philosophers assessed magical claims. A phenomenon could be miraculous (divine), natural (explicable through natural causes), or diabolical (a real effect produced through demonic cooperation or a demonic illusion). Aquinas's framework licensed the investigation of natural causes without immediately condemning them as demonic, while insisting that any operation requiring demonic cooperation was illicit.

Superstition and the Forbidden Arts

The Secunda secundae, qq. 92–96 define superstition (Latin superstitio) as a species of irreligion: the attribution to creatures of what belongs to God alone, or the worship of God in an improper manner. Divination (divinatio) is the attempt to know hidden or future things by means of creatures — stars, spirits, lots, dreams — rather than through divine revelation or legitimate causal reasoning. Aquinas condemns all forms of divination as implicitly or explicitly involving demonic pact, even when the practitioner does not consciously intend this: the desire to obtain occult knowledge from spiritual agents that are not God constitutes a tacit invitation to demonic assistance.

Observations (observationes) — magical rituals using material objects, words, or procedures — are similarly condemned when they operate through demonic agency rather than natural causes. However, Aquinas acknowledges that some material things have natural occult powers (occult qualities) that can produce unusual effects without supernatural intervention; his De occultis operibus naturae (a brief treatise addressed to a soldier) develops this naturalistic alternative more fully.

persons.name: Richard Kieckhefer
persons.description: Learned magic, necromancy, and the social history of medieval ritual texts.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Richard Kieckhefer is a historian of medieval religion and magic at Northwestern University, where he taught for over three decades before retirement. His scholarship has been central to establishing the history of medieval magic as a legitimate and rigorous subdiscipline of medieval studies, combining careful archival work with broad synthetic analysis. He received his doctoral training at the University of Texas at Austin and has published across the history of medieval religion, spirituality, and the relationship between official theology and popular practice.

Major Works

Magic in the Middle Ages (Cambridge University Press, 1989; revised edition 2000) is Kieckhefer's most widely read work and the standard introduction to the field. The book surveys the full range of medieval magical practice — from village charms and protective amulets through learned necromancy — and introduces the crucial analytical distinction between "common tradition" (widely shared magical practices embedded in everyday life) and "specific tradition" (the specialized learned magic of the educated clergy and university-trained). Kieckhefer's concept of the "clerical underworld" — the social milieu of clergy and university students who circulated practical magic manuscripts alongside more respectable texts — has been widely adopted and debated.

Forbidden Rites: A Necromancer's Manual of the Fifteenth Century (Penn State University Press, 1997) offers an edition, translation, and analysis of the Munich Manual (Clm 849), a Latin necromantic handbook from the 1440s. The edition is a model of how to approach a practical magic manuscript: Kieckhefer situates the text in its manuscript context, analyses its ritual structure and theoretical assumptions, and uses it to illuminate the social world of learned clerical magic. The book is essential reading for anyone working on the Latin grimoire tradition.

His edited volume Conjuring Spirits: Texts and Traditions of Medieval Ritual Magic (Penn State, 1994), co-edited with Claire Fanger, assembled key essays on medieval ritual magic and helped define the field's scope and methods. Theology in Stone: Church Architecture from Byzantium to Berkeley (2004) represents his parallel work on medieval religious culture. His work on medieval devotion and mysticism (Unquiet Souls: Fourteenth-Century Saints and their Religious Milieu, 1984; Mystics and Miracles, 2015) provides the broader religious-historical context within which the history of magic is properly situated.

persons.name: Claire Fanger
persons.description: Medieval ritual magic, angelic theurgy, and visionary autobiographical writing.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Claire Fanger is a scholar of medieval religion and ritual magic at Rice University whose editorial and interpretive work has been central to establishing the study of medieval ritual magic as a rigorous historical subdiscipline. Her work focuses on the intersection of magic, mysticism, and religious experience in the later Middle Ages, with particular attention to texts that blur the boundaries between legitimate contemplative practice and condemned magical operation.

Editorial Work

Fanger edited the landmark volume Conjuring Spirits: Texts and Traditions of Medieval Ritual Magic (Penn State University Press, 1998), which brought together essays on the Ars Notoria, the Munich Manual, the Liber visionum of John of Morigny, and other key texts, establishing the field's scope and methods. A follow-up volume, Invoking Angels: Theurgic Ideas and Practices, Thirteenth to Sixteenth Centuries (Penn State, 2012), extended the analysis to the relationship between angel magic and mysticism across three centuries.

Her edition (with Nicholas Watson) of John of Morigny's Liber florum celestis doctrine (The Flowers of Heavenly Teaching, Penn State, 2015) is the critical scholarly edition of this extraordinary visionary text, providing Latin text, English translation, and extensive introduction. The edition demonstrates the kind of careful textual and contextual analysis that distinguishes modern grimoire scholarship from earlier occultist editions.

Interpretive Contributions

Fanger's interpretive work addresses the relationship between magical and mystical traditions in medieval Christianity, arguing against sharp categorical distinctions between "magic" (condemned) and "mysticism" (approved). Her analysis of John of Morigny shows how a practitioner could engage with the Ars Notoria tradition, receive visionary critique of it, and produce a revised system that was itself neither purely magical nor purely contemplative. This blurring of categories is characteristic of the learned magical milieu and important for understanding how magical practice was experienced by its practitioners.

persons.name: Frank Klaassen
persons.description: Manuscript culture and transformations of learned magic in late medieval and early modern England.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Frank Klaassen is a historian of medieval magic and learned culture at the University of Saskatchewan. His research focuses on the practical ritual magic texts of medieval England — the manuscripts that circulated among literate clergy and university-trained practitioners — and on what their content and manuscript contexts reveal about the culture of learned magic in the later Middle Ages. He studied at the University of Toronto and completed his doctorate there.

The Transformations of Magic

The Transformations of Magic: Illicit Learned Magic in the Later Middle Ages (Penn State University Press, 2013) is Klaassen's major monograph and the most rigorous systematic study of the English learned magic manuscript tradition. The book surveys approximately 270 manuscripts containing ritual magic material, providing a quantitative foundation for generalizations about what types of magic circulated, in what social contexts, and how the tradition changed between c.1300 and c.1500. Klaassen identifies two transformations: a shift in some parts of the tradition toward more explicit demonic conjuration, and a counter-trend of naturalization in which ritual operations were increasingly framed within the idiom of scholastic natural philosophy and celestial influence theory.

The book's methodological contribution — the systematic manuscript survey rather than focus on a few canonical texts — was influential in subsequent grimoire scholarship, demonstrating that the selection bias of printed editions had significantly distorted earlier accounts of what medieval learned magic actually looked like.

Other Work

Klaassen has edited and introduced key primary texts in the medieval magic corpus. His edition (with Christopher Phillips) of the Ars Notoria tradition and his contributions to Claire Fanger's Invoking Angels (Penn State, 2012) expand the manuscript base for understanding angelic magic in the medieval period. He has also published on the relationship between learned magic and early modern print culture, on the transition from manuscript to print in the magical tradition, and on the Solomonic attribution as a legitimating strategy.
