persons.name: Marsilio Ficino
persons.description: Florentine philosopher, physician, and priest who directed Cosimo de' Medici's Platonic Academy and produced the first Latin translation of the Corpus Hermeticum (1463). Ficino's De Vita (1489), especially the third book De Vita Coelitus Comparanda, formulated an influential theory of stellar and spiritus magic drawing on Neoplatonism, astral medicine, and what he took to be ancient Hermetic wisdom. Frances Yates argued that Ficino inaugurated a distinctly Renaissance magical tradition; Frank Klaassen has argued the continuities with medieval learned magic are stronger than Yates recognized. D.P. Walker's Spiritual and Demonic Magic (1958) remains the standard treatment of Ficino's magical theory.
persons.bio_html:
Life

Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was born in Figline Valdarno, near Florence, the son of a physician who served the Medici. Cosimo de' Medici, recognizing the young scholar's promise, placed him under the tutelage of humanist teachers and eventually entrusted him with the translation of the newly acquired manuscripts of Plato and the Neoplatonists — a project that would occupy Ficino's entire career and reshape European intellectual life. Ficino spent most of his adult life at the Medici villa at Careggi, the nominal centre of what later scholars called the "Platonic Academy." He was ordained a priest in 1473, an event that introduced productive tensions between his philosophical commitments and his theological obligations that run through all his major works.

The Translation Project

Ficino's first major task, at Cosimo's urgent request, was to interrupt his Platonic translation project to render the newly arrived Corpus Hermeticum — fourteen Greek treatises attributed to Hermes Trismegistus — into Latin. This translation, completed in 1463 and circulated in manuscript before its 1471 printed edition, introduced the Hermetica to Latin Europe. Ficino accepted the traditional attribution: Hermes Trismegistus was, he believed, a real Egyptian sage of Mosaic antiquity, and the Hermetica preserved a primordial philosophical theology (prisca theologia) that anticipated Christian truth. This conviction structured his entire philosophical project: the recovery of ancient wisdom was also a preparation of pagan learning for Christian reception.

His translations of Plato's complete dialogues (1484), Plotinus's Enneads (1492), Iamblichus, Porphyry, Proclus, and Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite established Latin versions that remained standard for centuries. His commentaries — especially the Commentarium in Convivium Platonis de amore (1469, printed 1484) — transmitted Platonic philosophy in a form accessible to humanist readers across Europe.

Magia and De vita

The most controversial element of Ficino's intellectual production was the third book of his De vita trilogy, De vita coelitus comparanda (On Drawing Life from the Sky, 1489). Here Ficino outlined a system of therapeutic astral magic. The basis was Neoplatonic: the spiritus mundi, a subtle intermediary pervading the cosmos, linked the celestial bodies to all terrestrial things through bonds of sympathy and antipathy. A philosopher-physician — especially one of melancholic constitution (Saturn's children were the scholars and intellectuals) — could mitigate the excessive cold and dryness of Saturnine influence by attracting solar or Jovian spiritus through the use of appropriate materials: gold, amber, saffron, wine, images of the sun, solar music, exposure to sunlight and cheerful company.

D.P. Walker, in Spiritual and Demonic Magic from Ficino to Campanella (1958), was the first modern scholar to analyse this system in depth, arguing that it occupies an ambiguous position: Ficino consistently insisted that his magic operated through purely natural celestial causes, yet the Neoplatonic framework it drew on — especially from Iamblichus and Proclus — involved genuine spirit-working that could not easily be naturalised. Brian Copenhaver's subsequent work has been more sympathetic to Ficino's self-presentation as a natural philosopher, while acknowledging the philosophical instability of the position. The 1489 text caused Ficino genuine anxiety; he was investigated by the Florentine curia and appended a lengthy self-defence to subsequent editions.

Influence and Reception

Ficino's influence on the subsequent century of European thought was immense. Giovanni Pico della Mirandola absorbed and radicalised his synthesis, adding Christian Kabbalah. Lefèvre d'Étaples translated and promoted his work in France. Cornelius Agrippa's De occulta philosophia (1531) drew extensively on Ficino for its theory of the world-soul and elemental magic. John Colet in England and the German humanists engaged his Platonic commentaries. His influence on English Neoplatonism reached from the Cambridge Platonists of the seventeenth century to the Romantic poets.

For the history of magic specifically, the key secondary literature includes Brian Copenhaver's edition and translation of the Hermetica (1992) and his philosophical studies of Ficino's sources; D.P. Walker's foundational 1958 monograph; Michael Allen's work on Ficino's Platonic commentaries; and Stéphane Toussaint's studies of Ficino's natural magic and its reception.

persons.name: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola
persons.description: Italian Renaissance philosopher who attempted to synthesize Christian theology, Neoplatonism, Hermeticism, and Jewish Kabbalah. His 900 Theses (1486) and Oration on the Dignity of Man presented magic as a natural science capable of uniting all human knowledge. Pope Innocent VIII condemned thirteen of his theses. Pico distinguished magia naturalis from goetia and was among the first Renaissance writers to incorporate Hebrew Kabbalah into a Christian magical synthesis. His early death in 1494 left his synthesis incomplete but enormously influential on Agrippa, Trithemius, Dee, and later Renaissance occultists.

persons.name: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa
persons.description: German polymath and lawyer who produced the most comprehensive Renaissance synthesis of occult philosophy. De Occulta Philosophia circulated in manuscript from c.1510 and was published in Cologne in expanded form (1531-1533). Agrippa drew on Ficino, Pico, Trithemius, and medieval magical sources to construct a three-tiered system of natural, celestial, and ceremonial magic. Klaassen has shown that Agrippa's third book draws directly on late medieval demonic and angelic magic manuscripts, undermining the clean break often claimed between medieval and Renaissance magic. He was at various times physician, courtier, legal scholar, and itinerant lecturer across Germany, France, and Italy.
persons.bio_html:
Life

Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim (1486–1535) was born in Cologne into a minor noble family. His education at the University of Cologne gave him the Latin learning and Scholastic philosophy that underpin his major works, while his subsequent wandering career — soldier, diplomat, court physician, lecturer, and perennial debtor — exposed him to the intellectual currents of humanist Italy, French and English royal courts, and the reform milieu of early German Lutheranism. He served in Maximilian I's campaigns in northern Italy around 1511, where contact with Italian Platonists (including possibly pupils of Ficino's circle) sharpened his interest in occult philosophy. He lectured on Reuchlin's Kabbalistic works at Dôle in 1509 and at a young age completed a first draft of his encyclopedic De occulta philosophia.

De occulta philosophia

The De occulta philosophia libri tres, first circulated in manuscript from 1510 onward and finally published in 1531 (Cologne, Soter), is the most comprehensive synthesis of Renaissance occult philosophy: a structured encyclopedia covering all three "worlds" of the Neoplatonic cosmos. Book I treats natural magic — the occult properties of things in the elemental world, the four elements, the harmony of the macrocosm and microcosm, the magical use of stones, plants, metals, animals, and numbers. Book II treats celestial or mathematical magic — the influences of the seven planets, the fixed stars, and the signs of the zodiac; the construction of magical images and talismans; magical squares, the camea of the planets. Book III treats ceremonial or divine magic — the celestial hierarchy of angels and demons, divine names, the Kabbalah, the power of words and letters, ritual operations for drawing down divine assistance.

The work synthesizes an enormous range of sources: Ficino's Neoplatonism and astral medicine, Pico's Kabbalah, Trithemius on cryptography and angelic communication, pseudo-Albertus on occult properties, the Hermetic writings, Pliny, and Arabic astrological theory via al-Kindi and the Picatrix. Its ambition was not merely encyclopedic but philosophical: Agrippa wanted to demonstrate that a unified science of nature, properly understood, encompassed what the ignorant dismissed as superstition.

De incertitudine and the Sceptical Turn

The paradox of Agrippa's career is that his other major published work, De incertitudine et vanitate scientiarum et artium (1530, published slightly before De occulta philosophia), appears to repudiate everything the larger book argues for. De incertitudine is a Pyrrhonist satire attacking all human knowledge, including magic: Agrippa denounces the whole project of occult philosophy as vanity, asserting that only Scriptural revelation provides genuine knowledge. The relationship between the two works has been debated for centuries. Charles Nauert's Agrippa and the Crisis of Renaissance Thought (1965) remains the standard monograph. Paola Zambelli's work reassessed Agrippa's scepticism in the context of fideist theology and rhetorical strategies of self-protection.

Influence

Agrippa's influence was enormous and long-lasting. De occulta philosophia was reprinted throughout the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries; English versions circulated in manuscript before the 1651 printed edition (which included the spurious "Fourth Book"). John Dee owned copies and annotated them; the Elizabethan magus Simon Forman and others drew on it directly. Christopher Marlowe almost certainly drew on the Agrippa legend for Doctor Faustus (c.1592). The Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy, a demonic conjuration manual falsely appended to Agrippa's name, circulated from the 1550s, further complicating his posthumous reputation. His reputation as an extreme magician persisted long after his death.

persons.name: Johannes Trithemius
persons.name_alt: Johann von Trittenheim; Trithemius of Sponheim
persons.description: Benedictine abbot of Sponheim (1483-1505) and later Würzburg, legendary bibliophile who transformed Sponheim's library from fifty to over two thousand volumes. His Steganographia (c.1499, printed 1606) circulated in manuscript as an apparent manual of angel magic for long-distance communication; Book III was shown in 1998 to contain cryptographic ciphers beneath the magical text. His Polygraphia (1518) was the first printed cryptography manual. Trithemius was accused of necromancy and demonic magic but defended a restricted natural magic. Agrippa visited him in 1509-1510, and the meeting was formative for the composition of De Occulta Philosophia.
persons.bio_html:
Life

Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), born Johann Heidenberg in Trittenheim on the Moselle, was a Benedictine abbot, humanist scholar, encyclopedist, and occultist whose works bridged the learned worlds of humanism, monastic reform, and Renaissance magic. Elected abbot of Sponheim at the age of twenty-one, he transformed the monastery into a major intellectual centre with a library of over 2,000 volumes — remarkable by contemporary standards. He later served as abbot of Würzburg's St. James's. His correspondents included Agrippa, Erasmus, Conrad Celtis, and the Emperor Maximilian I.

Works

Trithemius produced an enormous range of writing. His Polygraphia (1518, posthumous) and Steganographia (written c.1499, not printed until 1606) are the most important for the history of magic and cryptography. The Steganographia presents itself as a system for communicating through spirits; its three books contain what appeared to be instructions for demonic conjuration, causing it to be placed on the Index of Prohibited Books. Modern scholars (Thomas Ernst and others) have demonstrated that the first two books contain a sophisticated polyalphabetic cipher hidden within the apparently magical instructions — a pioneering work in the history of cryptography — though Book III may contain genuine magical content.

The Polygraphia is an openly acknowledged treatise on steganography and substitution ciphers, the first printed book on cryptography. Trithemius's historical works, including the Annales Hirsaugienses and the Compendium sive Breviarium, are important for the history of German monasticism, though they are notorious for containing fabricated documents — Trithemius was willing to invent sources when genuine ones were unavailable, a practice that complicates his use as a historical authority.

Significance for Magic

Trithemius's early response to Cornelius Agrippa's manuscript of De occulta philosophia (1510) — cautious approval coupled with a warning about public disclosure — captures the ambivalence of the learned magical milieu: genuine intellectual engagement with magical philosophy alongside awareness of the risks of making it public. His own Steganographia exemplifies this: a text that circulated in manuscript for a century before print, widely known in magical circles, apparently revealing demonic secrets while concealing a purely technical cryptographic system.

persons.name: John Dee
persons.description: English mathematician, astrologer, and natural philosopher who assembled one of the largest private libraries in Elizabethan England at Mortlake, Surrey, with approximately 4,000 volumes including manuscripts of medieval magical texts. Dee's angel conversations with scryers including Bartholomew Hickman and Edward Kelley (1582-1589) produced the Mysteriorum Libri Quinque and the Enochian angelic language system. Frank Klaassen has demonstrated that Dee's magical practice was firmly grounded in late medieval demonic and angelic magic traditions, contradicting interpretations that see him as a pure Hermetic or Neoplatonist. Dee also had a hand in preserving three codices of image magic.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Career

John Dee (1527–1608/09) was the most intellectually formidable of Elizabethan England's learned magicians, a mathematical practitioner, natural philosopher, court astrologer, and angelic communicant whose career intersects with virtually every current of sixteenth-century occult philosophy. Born in Tower Ward, London, of Welsh descent, Dee entered St John's College Cambridge in 1542 and became a founding fellow of Trinity College in 1546. His early reputation was built on mathematical science: his 1570 "Mathematical Preface" to Henry Billingsley's English translation of Euclid is a landmark in the promotion of mathematics as a practical art of navigation, engineering, and natural inquiry.

Dee's library at Mortlake, accumulated over decades, was one of the largest private libraries in Elizabethan England — he estimated it at over 4,000 volumes in a 1583 petition — and served as both a research centre and a node in the European republic of letters. He corresponded with Ortelius, with Gerard Mercator (who gave him his projection globes), and with Continental scholars of natural philosophy and mathematics. His continental visits (1547–1548, 1562–1563, 1583–1589) placed him within networks extending to the Habsburg court.

Angel Magic and the Enochian System

The angel conversations, conducted from 1582 to 1589 with the scryer Edward Kelley as the primary medium, represent the most extensively documented angelic communication project in European history. Dee's diaries of the sessions (now principally British Library MS Sloane 3188, 3677, and the volumes published posthumously by Meric Casaubon in 1659 as A True and Faithful Relation) record hundreds of sessions in which Kelley, gazing into a crystal "shewstone," received messages from angelic communicants. These messages included the Enochian (or "Angelic") language — a complete constructed language with its own alphabet, grammar, and nineteen "Keys" or "Calls" — along with extensive eschatological prophecy, instructions on alchemical operations, and political advice concerning the Catholic powers threatening Protestant Europe.

Dee understood the angel conversations not as magical operations in the grimoiric sense (he consistently denied using demonic spirits) but as a divinely sanctioned programme of reformed natural philosophy: the angels, he believed, were restoring the pure Adamic knowledge of nature lost at the Fall, equipping him to reform learning and serve the Protestant cause. Deborah Harkness's John Dee's Conversations with Angels (1999) provides the most thorough analysis of this project, situating it within the context of Elizabethan natural philosophy, religious reform, and Dee's political ambitions. Glyn Parry's The Arch-Conjuror of England (2011) provides a more sceptical reading focused on Dee's court career and the political uses of his occult reputation.

Works and Manuscripts

Dee's published output is smaller than his manuscript production. The Propaedeumata Aphoristica (1558, rev. 1568) sets out his theory of rays and celestial influence. The Monas Hieroglyphica (Antwerp, 1564) — dedicated to Maximilian II — is an alchemical-Kabbalistic meditation on a single glyph that Dee believed compressed universal wisdom. The General and Rare Memorials pertaining to the Perfecte Arte of Navigation (1577) argued for a British empire based on naval supremacy and was explicitly political.

His manuscripts, widely scattered during his lifetime — his library was ransacked at Mortlake during his absence in 1583 — survive principally in the British Library (Sloane and Cotton collections), the Bodleian, and Trinity College Cambridge. The Cotton Appendix and the Royal College of Physicians MS preserve key records of the angelic conferences. Stephen Clucas has edited and analysed several important manuscript sources.

Scholarship

The historiography of Dee has moved through several phases. Frances Yates's treatment in The Rosicrucian Enlightenment (1972) placed him within a Hermetic-Rosicrucian network; this was contested by scholars who found the Rosicrucian connection anachronistic. Nicholas Clulee's John Dee's Natural Philosophy (1988) was the first comprehensive study to treat Dee's natural philosophy seriously on its own terms. Harkness (1999) and Parry (2011) represent the current state of Dee scholarship, from complementary perspectives.

persons.name: Edward Kelley
persons.description: English scryer and alchemist who served as John Dee's primary medium during the angelic conversations of 1582-1589. Kelley arrived at Dee's Mortlake home in March 1582 and served as the visionary intermediary through whose shewstone the angelic intelligences were seen and heard. The Enochian language and the associated tables of correspondences were developed through these sessions and recorded by Dee in the Mysteriorum Libri Quinque and related diaries. Kelley later separated from Dee and pursued alchemy in Bohemia under Emperor Rudolf II, where he died in prison in 1597. His claimed relationship to the angelic communications remains debated by historians.

persons.name: Giordano Bruno
persons.description: Italian Dominican friar, philosopher, and itinerant intellectual who synthesized Hermeticism, Neoplatonism, infinite cosmology, and mnemonic art. Frances Yates argued in Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition (1964) that Bruno was fundamentally a Hermetic Magus whose memory theater and cosmological innovations derived from Ficino's magical tradition and were central to the Scientific Revolution. Subsequent scholars have substantially revised this thesis while acknowledging Bruno's explicit engagement with astral magic sources including the Picatrix. He was burned at the stake in Rome in February 1600, condemned for heresies that may have included magical doctrines alongside his cosmological views.
persons.bio_html:
Life

Giordano Bruno (1548–1600) was born in Nola near Naples, entered the Dominican Order, and spent his career as a wandering philosopher, teacher, and controversial public figure in Toulouse, Geneva, Paris, London, Wittenberg, Prague, and Venice before his arrest by the Venetian Inquisition in 1592. He was transferred to Rome, held for seven years, and burned at the stake at the Campo de' Fiori on 17 February 1600. The specific charges on which he was condemned are not all known, but they included denying the Trinity, denying the Incarnation, denying transubstantiation, believing in the plurality of worlds and the eternity of matter, practising magic, and denying the divinity of Christ.

Hermetic Philosophy and Magic

Bruno's philosophy is, as Frances Yates argued in Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition (1964), fundamentally Hermetic: his panpsychic universe, in which the world-soul animates all things and matter is itself infused with intelligence, derives from the Corpus Hermeticum and from Ficino's reading of it. His works of the 1580s — the Italian philosophical dialogues (La cena de le ceneri, De la causa, principio et uno, De l'infinito, universo et mondi), the Latin treatises on magic (De magia, De vinculis in genere, Theses de magia), and the Latin memory treatises (De umbris idearum, Cantus Circaeus) — constitute the most philosophically ambitious engagement with Hermetic magic in the Renaissance.

Bruno's theory of magic in De magia and De vinculis moves beyond Ficinian natural magic toward a theory of what he calls "bonds" — the connections through which the magician operates on other minds and souls. The magician does not merely manipulate physical forces; he understands and exploits the passions, desires, and imaginative susceptibilities of others. This psychological theory of magic anticipates modern theories of rhetoric, persuasion, and charisma.

Legacy

Bruno became a martyr figure for Italian nationalism in the nineteenth century (a statue stands at the Campo de' Fiori) and for subsequent freethinkers. His philosophical legacy has been disputed: Yates argued that his Hermeticism was central to the Scientific Revolution; others have argued that his specific cosmological claims (infinite universe, plurality of worlds) were reached by philosophical reasoning rather than magic. Ioan Couliano's Eros and Magic in the Renaissance (1987) provides the most ambitious recent interpretation of his theory of magic.

persons.name: Giovanni Battista della Porta
persons.description: Neapolitan natural philosopher, playwright, and polymath who compiled Magia Naturalis (first edition 1558, expanded four-book version 1589). Della Porta articulated a systematic natural philosophy of sympathies, antipathies, and occult properties, incorporating phenomena previously attributed to magical or demonic agency into natural explanation. He founded the Accademia dei Segreti (Academy of Secrets) in Naples and was investigated by the Inquisition. His work represents the interface between late Renaissance natural philosophy and the grimoire tradition, exemplifying how the concept of magia naturalis expanded to include observational, experimental, and artisanal knowledge under a single rubric derived from natural philosophy.

persons.name: Frances Yates
persons.description: British historian of Renaissance culture associated with the Warburg Institute, London. Her Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition (1964) argued that Hermeticism and natural magic were central to Renaissance intellectual culture and causally linked to the Scientific Revolution. Her related studies The Art of Memory (1966), The Rosicrucian Enlightenment (1972), and The Occult Philosophy in the Elizabethan Age (1979) extended this framework. The Yates thesis held that Ficino and Pico transmitted an ancient Hermetic-magical wisdom that renewed and transformed both natural philosophy and occult practice; this argument was challenged by Vickers, Copenhaver, and Klaassen, but it transformed the historiography of Renaissance magic and remains a necessary reference point.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Career

Dame Frances Amelia Yates (1899–1981) was one of the most influential historians of Renaissance thought in the twentieth century, whose work transformed the study of the relationship between magic, Hermeticism, and the history of science. She was educated privately and at University College London (BA, 1924; MA, 1926), never holding a doctorate but spending her career at the Warburg Institute in London, where she rose from research associate (1941) to Reader (1956) and ultimately Honorary Fellow. Her career exemplifies the Warburg Institute's distinctive method: rigorous archival research in the iconographic and textual traditions of Renaissance Europe, guided by the conviction that images, symbols, and philosophical programmes were as historically significant as political or economic events.

Major Works

Yates's scholarly production falls into two broad phases. Her early work focused on the French and English Renaissance, producing studies of the Académie de Poésie et de Musique (The French Academies of the Sixteenth Century, 1947), John Florio (A Study of Love's Labour's Lost, 1936), and the Elizabethan court festival (Astraea: The Imperial Theme in the Sixteenth Century, 1975). Her method in these works — close reading of complex symbolic programmes in theatrical performances, court masques, and emblematic visual culture — gave her the tools she would bring to Hermeticism.

The second and most influential phase began with Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition (Routledge, 1964), in which she argued that Bruno's philosophical system was fundamentally Hermetic rather than proto-scientific, and that the recovery of the Corpus Hermeticum by Ficino in 1463 inaugurated a tradition of "Hermetic" thought that ran through the Renaissance and into the seventeenth century, contributing to the emergence of what she called "the Rosicrucian enlightenment." The Art of Memory (1966) traced the ancient and Renaissance tradition of the memory systems from Cicero through Ramon Llull, Giulio Camillo's memory theatre, and Bruno's mnemonic works, arguing that the art of memory was deeply implicated in magical and Hermetic thinking. The Rosicrucian Enlightenment (1972) extended the argument into the early seventeenth century, linking the anonymous Rosicrucian manifestos (1614–1616) to the Palatine court of Frederick V and Elizabeth Stuart and to a utopian programme of Hermetic reform that Yates connected to Francis Bacon and early modern science.

The Yates Thesis and Its Afterlife

The central claim of the "Yates thesis" — that Hermetic magic provided crucial psychological and conceptual preconditions for the Scientific Revolution — was debated intensely from the 1970s onward. Brian Vickers, Robert Westman, David Lindberg, and others argued that the thesis overstated Hermeticism's role and understated the continuities with Scholastic Aristotelian natural philosophy. The specific claim about Hermeticism's causal role in Copernicanism (Yates had suggested Bruno influenced Copernicus's heliocentric commitment) was largely abandoned. Yet the broader achievement — establishing the study of Renaissance magic and esotericism as a legitimate historical discipline, and demonstrating that Hermetic and occult traditions deserved the same rigorous historical attention as mathematical astronomy or Protestant theology — remains acknowledged as a foundational contribution.

Yates was appointed OBE in 1972 and DBE in 1977. She received honorary degrees from Edinburgh, Essex, East Anglia, and Exeter. Her papers are held at the Warburg Institute.

persons.name: D.P. Walker
persons.description: British historian at the Warburg Institute whose Spiritual and Demonic Magic: From Ficino to Campanella (1958) gave the first systematic scholarly treatment to Renaissance magic's relationship with Neoplatonism and demonology. Walker distinguished spiritual magic, which operates through the spiritus or pneuma mediating between soul and body in Ficino's sense, from demonic magic involving explicit demonic summoning. His nuanced framework preceded and shaped Frances Yates's more sweeping arguments and remains the standard scholarly account of Ficino's De Vita Coelitus Comparanda as a magical text. Walker also published on music therapy in the Renaissance and on unorthodox religious thought.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Daniel Pickering Walker (1914–1985) was a British intellectual historian at the Warburg Institute in London whose work on Renaissance music theory, Orphic singing, and spiritual magic established the scholarly foundation for the study of Renaissance occult philosophy a decade before Frances Yates's more publicly celebrated syntheses. Walker studied at Oxford and at the École Normale Supérieure in Paris, and spent his career at the Warburg Institute, where he was a colleague and close associate of Yates.

Spiritual and Demonic Magic

Spiritual and Demonic Magic from Ficino to Campanella (Warburg Institute, 1958; reprinted Penn State University Press, 2000) is Walker's masterpiece and the foundational text of modern scholarship on Renaissance learned magic. The book asks a focused philosophical question: how did Renaissance Neoplatonist magicians attempt to distinguish their operations from demonic magic, and how successful were these attempts? Walker traces the problem through Ficino's De vita coelitus comparanda, Pico della Mirandola, Francesco Giorgi, Cornelius Agrippa, Giambattista della Porta, and Giordano Bruno, showing in each case both the sophistication of the attempt to naturalize magical operations and the points at which the naturalization broke down.

Walker's central insight — that the Neoplatonic framework Ficino used to explain astral magic was not entirely innocent of the demonic implications it was meant to avoid, because it derived from Iamblichus and Proclus, who had themselves discussed the role of daemons in theurgic operations — remained the defining problem of Renaissance magic scholarship for two decades. His careful philosophical reading, his attention to what Renaissance thinkers actually wrote rather than what later interpreters wanted them to have written, and his refusal of grand causal claims set a standard that subsequent work has either followed or had to argue against.

Other Work

Walker's other major work is The Ancient Theology: Studies in Christian Platonism from the Fifteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1972), which traces the tradition of prisca theologia (primordial theology) and its relationship to Renaissance and later thought. His posthumously collected essays on music and magic, edited by Penelope Gouk as Music, Spirit and Language in the Renaissance (1985), extend the concerns of the 1958 monograph into the domain of musical theory and its magical applications — Ficino's Orphic singing, the power of music to affect the spirits and passions.

persons.name: Owen Davies
persons.description: British historian at the University of Hertfordshire specializing in the social and cultural history of magic, witchcraft, and folk religion from the early modern period to the present. His Grimoires: A History of Magic Books (Oxford University Press, 2009) provides the most comprehensive survey of grimoire transmission from late antiquity to the twenty-first century, covering the printing press, vernacular diffusion, popular magic, and contemporary usage. Davies has also published on cunning folk in early modern England, the global spread of magical texts in colonial and postcolonial contexts, and popular witchcraft beliefs. His work bridges the gap between medieval manuscript studies and the social history of popular magic.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Owen Davies is Professor of Social History at the University of Hertfordshire and the leading historian of popular and print magic in modern Britain and the English-speaking world. His scholarship spans the history of witchcraft, cunning folk, ghosts, and magical books in Britain and America, with particular attention to the intersection of print culture, popular belief, and learned tradition in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

Major Works

Grimoires: A History of Magic Books (Oxford University Press, 2009) is Davies's most synthetic work and the essential scholarly history of the grimoire as a genre from antiquity to the present. The book traces the transformation of learned magical manuscripts into commercial print publications, from the early modern chapbook grimoires of France (Grand Albert, Petit Albert) through the nineteenth-century occult revival editions (Mathers, Waite) and the twentieth-century paperback grimoire market, showing how each phase of print technology and each social context produced grimoires adapted to its conditions.

Popular Magic: Cunning-folk in English History (Hambledon Continuum, 2003) documents the world of English cunning folk — the village-level magical practitioners who provided healing, divination, and counter-magic services — from the sixteenth through the nineteenth centuries. The book demonstrates, against the long-standing assumption that learned magic and popular magic were entirely separate spheres, that cunning folk regularly used printed and manuscript magical texts, including grimoires, as resources for their practice.

America Bewitched: The Story of Witchcraft after Salem (Oxford, 2013) extends this analysis to North America, tracing the persistence of witchcraft belief and practice through the nineteenth century and into the twentieth. Earlier works include Witchcraft, Magic and Culture 1736–1951 (Manchester, 1999) and The Haunted: A Social History of Ghosts (Palgrave, 2007).

persons.name: Joseph H. Peterson
persons.description: American editor and archivist who founded esotericarchives.com (1995), the most comprehensive online repository of transcribed historical magical texts. Peterson's critical editions include The Lesser Key of Solomon (2001), Grimorium Verum (2007), John Dee's Five Books of Mystery: Mysteriorum Libri Quinque (2003), and The Sworn Book of Honorius (2016). His editions bring rigorous philological practice to texts long circulating in corrupt printed forms, comparing manuscript witnesses to establish reliable texts with scholarly apparatus. Peterson is also co-editor of The Book of Oberon (2015, with Daniel Harms and James R. Clark), the edition of the Folger Shakespeare Library's Elizabethan manuscript of conjuring and fairy magic.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Work

Joseph Peterson is an independent scholar and editor whose Esoteric Archives project (online from 1997 at esotericarchives.com) and subsequent print editions through Ibis Press and Teitan Press have produced the most rigorous modern scholarly editions of the Solomonic and related grimoire corpus. His work represents a decisive advance over the nineteenth-century occultist editions of Mathers, Waite, and their contemporaries: Peterson works systematically from primary manuscripts, documents his sources, identifies variant readings, and situates texts in their manuscript traditions with reference to modern paleographic and philological standards.

Major Editions

His edition and translation of the Grimorium Verum (Ibis Press, 2007) provided the first reliable modern text of this eighteenth-century French grimoire. His edition of the Lemegeton Clavicula Salomonis (Weiser, 2001) — incorporating the Ars Goetia, Ars Theurgia-Goetia, Ars Paulina, Ars Almadel, and Ars Notoria — replaced Mathers's 1904 conflation with a careful documentary edition tracking the separate manuscript traditions of each component text. His Key of Solomon the King (Weiser, 2004) supersedes Mathers's 1888 edition by identifying and working from a broader range of manuscripts, including several not previously used in English-language scholarship.

The Esoteric Archives website provides free access to transcribed texts, manuscript images, and critical apparatus for dozens of texts in the Solomonic, Hermetic, and astrological magic traditions, making Peterson's work essential infrastructure for the scholarly study of the grimoire corpus. His collaboration with Dan Harms on The Long-Lost Friend (Llewellyn, 2012) — a scholarly edition of John George Hohman's 1820 Pennsylvania German magical handbook — demonstrates the same philological rigour applied to American folk magic.

persons.name: Dan Harms
persons.description: American librarian and scholar based in New York whose major research area is the history of magic from antiquity to the present, with particular attention to necromancy, fairy magic, and grimoire transmission. Harms is co-editor of The Book of Oberon: A Sourcebook of Elizabethan Magic (Llewellyn, 2015, with James R. Clark and Joseph H. Peterson), a transcription and annotated translation of Folger MS Vb.26, a late sixteenth-century English manuscript combining Solomonic spirit lists with vernacular fairy magic and practical conjuring. He has also edited The Long-Lost Friend (Llewellyn, 2012) and published articles in the Journal for the Academic Study of Magic, Abraxas, and Fortean Times.

persons.name: Francis Barrett
persons.description: English occultist and author of The Magus, or Celestial Intelligencer (London, 1801), a substantial compilation drawing heavily on Agrippa's De Occulta Philosophia, Robert Turner's translations of magical texts, and related Renaissance and medieval sources. Barrett's work marks the transition from the circulation of learned magic in manuscript and early print to Romantic-era occultism and is an early example of the commercial popularization of the grimoire tradition. He is reported to have run practical classes in occult philosophy in London. The Magus served as a conduit bringing Agrippa's system and related Renaissance material to nineteenth-century audiences before the Golden Dawn produced more scholarly treatments.

persons.name: Samuel Liddell MacGregor Mathers
persons.description: Scottish occultist and a founder of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn (1888). Mathers produced influential editions of medieval and early modern magical texts that introduced them to a wide English audience: The Key of Solomon the King (1888, translated from British Library manuscripts), The Book of the Sacred Magic of Abramelin the Mage (1898, from a French manuscript), and The Goetia: The Lesser Key of Solomon the King (1904, with Aleister Crowley). His editorial choices, invented sections, and translations significantly shaped twentieth-century reception of the grimoire tradition. Joseph Peterson's later critical editions have corrected many of Mathers's departures from manuscript sources.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Career

Samuel Liddell MacGregor Mathers (1854–1918) was a British occultist, ritual magician, and co-founder of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn who produced the most influential modern editions of several core Solomonic grimoires. Born Samuel Liddell Mathers in London (he added "MacGregor" to assert a Scottish Highland identity), he was a founder member of the Golden Dawn in 1888 and became its dominant intellectual figure, claiming authority over the order through communication with "Secret Chiefs" — superhuman adepts he alleged to have contacted in Paris.

Grimoire Editions

Mathers's editorial work on the Solomonic corpus was the most consequential aspect of his legacy for subsequent grimoire scholarship. His The Key of Solomon the King (Clavicula Salomonis) (Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner, 1888) was the first modern printed edition in English, based on British Museum manuscripts (principally Lansdowne MSS 1202, 1203, and Sloane 1307, 2383). Although the edition combined several divergent manuscript families without adequate documentation of their textual relationships, it made the Clavicula accessible to English-speaking practitioners and scholars for the first time and established the text's centrality to the late Victorian occult revival.

His translation of the Book of the Sacred Magic of Abramelin the Mage (Kegan Paul, 1898), based on a French manuscript (Bibliothèque de l'Arsenal MS 2351) and wrongly dated by Mathers to c.1458 (the text is now thought to originate in the early fifteenth century), introduced the eighteen-month "Abramelin operation" — a structured programme of prayer, purification, and ultimately demonic subjugation — to the English occult tradition. Aleister Crowley's 1899 experience of the Abramelin working, based on Mathers's translation, was seminal in his development as a magical practitioner and in the transmission of the text to twentieth-century ceremonial magic.

Influence

Mathers's Golden Dawn initiated figures including W.B. Yeats, Aleister Crowley, Arthur Machen, and Evelyn Underhill. His magical and editorial work shaped the entire subsequent tradition of Anglophone ceremonial magic. The scholarly assessment of his editorial work has been mixed: he was a genuine scholar of French, Latin, and Hebrew, but he worked before the development of modern textual criticism, and his conflated editions have caused bibliographic problems that Joseph Peterson's modern critical editions have had to correct systematically.

persons.name: Paracelsus
persons.name_alt: Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim
persons.description: Swiss-German physician, alchemist, and natural philosopher who rejected Galenic medicine and scholastic Aristotelianism in favor of a doctrine of correspondences, signatures, and elemental spirits. Paracelsus postulated gnomes, undines, sylphs, and salamanders as natural beings inhabiting the four elements, a framework that influenced later spirit magic traditions. His medical and philosophical works circulated widely from the later sixteenth century and contributed to an expanded magia naturalis incorporating alchemical operations. His relationship to the grimoire tradition is indirect but significant: Paracelsian natural philosophy provided intellectual resources for later vernacular magic practitioners and contributed to the Rosicrucian synthesis of the early seventeenth century.

persons.name: Reginald Scot
persons.description: English gentleman and writer who published The Discoverie of Witchcraft (London, 1584), the most important English-language skeptical critique of witch-hunting in the sixteenth century. Scot argued systematically that witchcraft accusations rested on fraud, delusion, and clerical manipulation. The Discoverie also preserved extensive descriptions of conjuring practice, spirit magic, and Solomonic procedures, making it an inadvertent sourcebook for later grimoire compilers. Klaassen notes that the book's publishers reissued it at mid-century recognizing its value to magical practitioners. King James VI of Scotland, who took witchcraft seriously, is reported to have ordered copies burned, though this is debated.

persons.name: Johann Weyer
persons.description: Dutch physician and skeptic who studied under Agrippa and published De Praestigiis Daemonum et Incantationibus ac Veneficiis (Basel, 1563). Weyer argued that confessions of witchcraft reflected delusion and disease rather than real demonic pacts; accused women lacked the intellectual and spiritual capacity for genuine demonic compacts. He accepted demonic existence while denying effective human magic, a position that allowed him to challenge witch-hunting while remaining within orthodox Christian demonology. His work drew on medical and theological authorities including his teacher Agrippa. Weyer influenced Reginald Scot and represents a significant strand of Renaissance critical engagement with learned demonology.

persons.name: Pablo Torijano
persons.description: Specialist in the esoteric traditions associated with Solomon in late antique and medieval Jewish, Christian, and Islamic sources. His Solomon the Esoteric King (2002) traces how the biblical king became a master of angels, demons, and occult knowledge, fundamentally reshaping scholarly understanding of Solomonic textual authority across religious boundaries.

persons.name: Gideon Bohak
persons.description: Professor of Jewish philosophy at Tel Aviv University and leading authority on ancient Jewish magic. His Ancient Jewish Magic: A History (Cambridge, 2008) provides the most comprehensive account of Jewish magical practice from antiquity through the rabbinic period, treating amulets, adjurations, Solomonic traditions, and the multilingual magical papyri that document a shared Mediterranean magical culture.

persons.name: Dennis C. Duling
persons.description: New Testament scholar and translator of the Testament of Solomon in James Charlesworth's Old Testament Pseudepigrapha (Doubleday, 1983). Duling's annotated translation made the Testament accessible to mainstream biblical scholarship and remains the standard English edition, contextualizing the text within first-century Jewish and Christian demonological thought and Solomonic legend.

persons.name: Herman Gollancz
persons.description: British rabbi and orientalist (1852–1930) who edited the Hebrew Mafteah Shelomoh (Key of Solomon) from the British Museum manuscript (Oriental MS 14759) for the Oriental Translation Fund (1914). Gollancz's edition was the first critical edition of a Hebrew recension of the Clavicula Salomonis, establishing that Hebrew versions of the Key of Solomon circulated independently of the Latin tradition and preserving Solomonic ritual formulas in their original linguistic setting.

persons.name: Michael A. Morgan
persons.description: Scholar who produced the first English translation of Sepher ha-Razim (The Book of Mysteries) published by the Society of Biblical Literature in 1983. Morgan's translation of Mordecai Margalioth's 1966 critical Hebrew edition made this foundational Jewish magical text available to English-language scholars of late antique and medieval magic, enabling comparative study of its angel hierarchies and Solomonic framework with Latin and Greek magical traditions.

persons.name: Étienne Tempier
persons.description: Bishop of Paris (d. 1279) whose condemnations of 1270 (13 theses) and 1277 (219 theses) defined the institutional limits of scholastic natural philosophy, including the condemnation of astrological determinism, the claim that celestial bodies determine terrestrial events, and related propositions that bore on learned magic. The 1277 condemnations reshaped the intellectual context for all subsequent medieval treatments of divination, image magic, and natural magical theory.

concepts.label: Medieval Magic
concepts.definition_short: Medieval magic is an Analyst Term for practices, accusations, texts, and learned theories that modern scholars group under magic while medieval actors used more specific categories such as nigromantia, superstitio, experimentum, and scientia imaginum.
concepts.significance: Medieval magic is an Analyst Term for practices, accusations, texts, and learned theories that modern scholars group under magic while medieval actors used more specific categories such as nigromantia, superstitio, experimentum, and scientia imaginum.

concepts.label: Ars Notoria
concepts.definition_short: Ars Notoria is an Actor Term for a medieval ritual art of learning that joined prayers, notae, angelic invocation, and claims of accelerated intellectual acquisition.
concepts.significance: Ars Notoria is an Actor Term for a medieval ritual art of learning that joined prayers, notae, angelic invocation, and claims of accelerated intellectual acquisition.

concepts.label: Nigromantia
concepts.definition_short: Nigromantia is a medieval Latin Actor Term often used for illicit ritual operations involving spirits, frequently blurred by clerical writers with necromancy and demonic magic.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Actor Term. Nigromantia is the medieval Latin term for demonic conjuration — the ritual summoning and commanding of demons. Although etymologically from Greek nekromanteia (divination through the dead), medieval Latin writers consistently glossed the term as "black art" (nigra ars), connecting the first element to Latin niger (black) rather than Greek nekros (dead). This folk etymology — which Isidore of Seville had already offered — transformed the meaning of the term: nigromantia in medieval learned usage designated not ghost-consultation but the entire complex of demonic conjuration, illusion, and operation through demonic power.

The Nigromancer in Medieval Culture

The figure of the nigromancer in medieval learned culture was typically imagined as a learned cleric: a man with Latin literacy who had access to the manuscripts containing conjuration procedures, knowledge of the ritual requirements (magic circles, fumigations, special garments, complex formulae), and the ability to perform the rites. This is the "clerical underworld" identified by Richard Kieckhefer: a penumbra of educated clergymen and university graduates whose social position and economic vulnerability made the practice of magic — offering services of divination, love magic, healing, or harm — attractive as a supplementary livelihood.

The Munich Manual (Clm 849), the principal surviving medieval Latin handbook of demonic conjuration, is addressed to exactly this figure: a literate clergyman with access to appropriate ritual materials, willing to perform procedures involving demonic pact in exchange for practical results. Kieckhefer's edition (Forbidden Rites, 1997) remains the essential analysis.

Condemnation and Persistence

Despite consistent ecclesiastical condemnation — from Isidore's taxonomy of forbidden arts through the inquisitorial manuals of the fifteenth century — nigromantic practice persisted in manuscript culture throughout the medieval period. The social conditions that sustained it (literate but economically marginal clergy, demand for magical services from laypeople, relative difficulty of detection when practices were performed privately) were not abolished by theological condemnation. The transition to print, documented by Owen Davies (Grimoires, 2009), transformed rather than ended the tradition.
concepts.significance: Nigromantia is a medieval Latin Actor Term often used for illicit ritual operations involving spirits, frequently blurred by clerical writers with necromancy and demonic magic.

concepts.label: Astral Image Magic
concepts.definition_short: Astral image magic is an Analyst Term for learned practices that connect images, planetary timing, materials, and celestial influence in Arabic and Latin scholastic settings.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Analyst Term. Astral image magic designates procedures in which an image — typically a figure sculpted in metal, wax, or another material — is created and consecrated under specific astrological conditions (appropriate planetary hour, sign, and configuration) in order to attract and concentrate the influence of a celestial body and direct it toward a practical end. The image functions as a material focal point for stellar power: its form, material, timing, and associated ritual (fumigation, prayer, inscription of divine or stellar names) constitute a complete technology of celestial mediation.

Sources

Astral image magic in medieval Latin culture derived primarily from Arabic sources translated in the twelfth century: al-Kindi's De radiis (On Rays), Thabit ibn Qurra's De imaginibus (On Images), and the Picatrix (Arabic Ghāyat al-ḥakīm). These texts provided the theoretical apparatus (stellar rays as the medium of celestial influence) and the practical instructions (which planets govern which operations, which materials and images are appropriate, which prayers and fumigations attract planetary spiritus). The Picatrix in particular — a vast compilation organized around the twenty-eight lunar mansions and seven planets — became the most comprehensive resource for astral image magic in the Latin learned tradition.

The Scholastic Problem

Astral image magic posed a specific and persistent problem for scholastic natural philosophy. If the images worked through purely natural celestial causes — attracting and concentrating stellar influence in the way a lens concentrates light — they were potentially licit: natural philosophy could study and even use natural forces without moral hazard. But if they required the invocation of planetary spirits as personal, rational agents — or if the inscribed names and characters had no natural basis but presupposed demonic assistance — they were operations of demonic magic condemned by Aquinas and canon law.

Nicolas Weill-Parot's concept of "addressative magic" (magie addressative), developed in his Les "images astrologiques" au Moyen Âge et à la Renaissance (2002), captures this distinction: magic is addressative when it explicitly addresses (speaks to, invokes, commands) spiritual agents as personal beings, rather than simply exploiting impersonal natural forces. Weill-Parot's argument is that the scholastic condemnation of image magic targeted specifically the addressative dimension, and that the naturalization strategies of Albertus Magnus and others were attempts to preserve image magic by removing or minimizing its addressative character.
concepts.significance: Astral image magic is an Analyst Term for learned practices that connect images, planetary timing, materials, and celestial influence in Arabic and Latin scholastic settings.

concepts.label: Picatrix Tradition
concepts.definition_short: The Picatrix tradition denotes the Arabic-to-Latin transmission of the Ghayat al-hakim and its reception as a major source for medieval and Renaissance astral magic.
concepts.significance: The Picatrix tradition denotes the Arabic-to-Latin transmission of the Ghayat al-hakim and its reception as a major source for medieval and Renaissance astral magic.

concepts.label: Grimoire
concepts.definition_short: Grimoire is primarily an Analyst Term for manuscript or printed collections of ritual instructions, spirit lists, conjurations, prayers, and experiments.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Actor and Analyst Term. "Grimoire" (from Old French grammaire, meaning a book of Latin grammar, hence any learned, mysterious book) designates a text containing magical procedures: conjurations, spells, ritual instructions, spirit catalogues, sigils, and related material. In actor-usage across the early modern period, practitioners spoke of their "books of magic," "books of experiments," or specific titles (Clavicula Salomonis, Lemegeton); "grimoire" became the common generic term only in the eighteenth century. As an analyst category, it covers a wide range from sophisticated learned compilations in Latin to simple vernacular pamphlets of popular magic.

The Genre

Grimoires as a genre share certain structural features regardless of their intellectual level: an authorizing frame (attribution to a great magician, king, or angel; a narrative of discovery or transmission); practical content (procedures for achieving specific ends — finding treasure, compelling love, harming enemies, achieving invisibility); often, a theoretical or cosmological framework (angelology, demonology, astrology) that explains why the procedures work; and typically, ritual preparation requirements (fasting, prayer, purity, timing by planetary hours).

The range within the genre is vast. At the learned end: Agrippa's De occulta philosophia (1531), a comprehensive philosophical synthesis; the Hygromanteia, a sophisticated Greek astrological manual; the Liber Razielis, a Hebrew-Latin compilation with kabbalistic elements. At the popular end: the Petit Albert and Grand Albert French chapbook grimoires of the eighteenth century, designed for a literate popular audience; the Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses, a mid-nineteenth-century German compilation that spread through immigrant communities.

Scholarship

Owen Davies's Grimoires: A History of Magic Books (Oxford University Press, 2009) provides the most comprehensive historical survey of the grimoire from antiquity to the present, tracing the transformation of the genre across print cultures and social contexts. Richard Kieckhefer's Forbidden Rites (1997) and Frank Klaassen's The Transformations of Magic (2013) cover the medieval Latin tradition. Dan Harms and Joe Lures's The Book of Oberon (2015) provides a scholarly edition of an Elizabethan English grimoire. Joseph Peterson's Esoteric Archives (online) and Ibis Press editions have made many primary texts available in critical editions for the first time.
concepts.significance: Grimoire is primarily an Analyst Term for manuscript or printed collections of ritual instructions, spirit lists, conjurations, prayers, and experiments.

concepts.label: Superstitio
concepts.definition_short: Superstitio is a Latin Actor Term used by theologians and pastoral writers to classify improper religious practice, divination, charms, and illicit ritual dependence.
concepts.significance: Superstitio is a Latin Actor Term used by theologians and pastoral writers to classify improper religious practice, divination, charms, and illicit ritual dependence.

concepts.label: Learned Magic
concepts.definition_short: Learned magic is an Analyst Term for textually transmitted practices cultivated by literate clerical, university, monastic, or courtly actors.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Analyst Term. "Learned magic" designates the magical practices, texts, and traditions associated with literate, educated practitioners — primarily clergy, university graduates, and court-connected scholars — as opposed to the protective charms, folk healing practices, and oral traditions associated with popular or village magic. The distinction is an analyst category: historical actors did not use the term "learned magic," and the boundary between learned and popular practice was permeable in both directions (charms circulated in written form; grimoires informed popular healing practice). Nevertheless, the analytical distinction captures something real about the different social contexts, material conditions (expensive manuscripts, specialized instruments), and theoretical ambitions of the grimoire tradition.

Characteristics

Learned magic in the medieval period is characterised by several features that distinguish it from popular magical practice. First, it is primarily textual: it depends on written books (grimoires, magical treatises, experiment collections) that require literacy, often in Latin, for their use. Second, it is theoretically self-aware: learned magical texts typically provide or assume a theoretical framework — Neoplatonic, Aristotelian, or astrological — that explains why the procedures work. Third, it tends toward systematic elaboration: the spirit catalogues, the hierarchies of angels and demons, the tables of planetary correspondences that characterise Solomonic and astrological magic represent a drive toward comprehensive ordering that is characteristic of scholastic and university culture. Fourth, it is socially ambitious: learned magicians presented themselves as operating at the top of a hierarchy of knowledge, not as village healers or cunning folk.

Social History

Richard Kieckhefer's Magic in the Middle Ages (1989) proposed the concept of the "clerical underworld" to describe the social milieu of learned magic: a penumbra of clergy, university students, and court-connected intellectuals who circulated practical magic texts alongside more respectable learned works. Frank Klaassen's The Transformations of Magic (2013) provides the most systematic evidence-based account of this milieu in the medieval English context. Sophie Page's Magic in the Cloister (2013) documents the specific role of monastic libraries and scribal culture in preserving and transmitting magical texts.

The boundaries between learned magic and natural philosophy were contested throughout the medieval and early modern periods. Scholars like Albertus Magnus and Roger Bacon included discussions of magical phenomena within their natural philosophical works, both expanding the domain of admissible enquiry and policing its borders by distinguishing natural from demonic causes. This ongoing negotiation between learned magic and natural philosophy is a central theme of Klaassen's work and of Nicolas Weill-Parot's studies of scholastic engagement with image magic.
concepts.significance: Learned magic is an Analyst Term for textually transmitted practices cultivated by literate clerical, university, monastic, or courtly actors.

concepts.label: Familiar Spirit
concepts.definition_short: Familiar spirit is an Actor Term in many late medieval and early modern contexts for a spirit bound to, assisting, or repeatedly contacted by a practitioner; modern scholars use the category cautiously because legal, literary, and ritual sources describe such spirits in different registers.
concepts.significance: Familiar spirit is an Actor Term in many late medieval and early modern contexts for a spirit bound to, assisting, or repeatedly contacted by a practitioner; modern scholars use the category cautiously because legal, literary, and ritual sources describe such spirits in different registers.

concepts.label: Magic and Cognition
concepts.definition_short: Magic and cognition is an Analyst Term for scholarship that studies medieval magical practice through memory, perception, learning, ritual attention, and the mental operations implied by diagrams, prayers, images, and repeated procedures.
concepts.significance: Magic and cognition is an Analyst Term for scholarship that studies medieval magical practice through memory, perception, learning, ritual attention, and the mental operations implied by diagrams, prayers, images, and repeated procedures.

concepts.label: Manuscript Miscellany
concepts.definition_short: Manuscript miscellany is an Analyst Term for codices that collect heterogeneous texts; in medieval magic scholarship it matters because ritual, medical, devotional, astrological, and divinatory materials often survive together rather than in isolated genre books.
concepts.significance: Manuscript miscellany is an Analyst Term for codices that collect heterogeneous texts; in medieval magic scholarship it matters because ritual, medical, devotional, astrological, and divinatory materials often survive together rather than in isolated genre books.

concepts.label: Clerical Underworld
concepts.definition_short: Clerical underworld is an Analyst Term associated especially with Richard Kieckhefer's account of literate clerics who copied, adapted, and used illicit ritual texts while remaining within ecclesiastical culture.
concepts.significance: Clerical underworld is an Analyst Term associated especially with Richard Kieckhefer's account of literate clerics who copied, adapted, and used illicit ritual texts while remaining within ecclesiastical culture.

concepts.label: Angelic Invocation
concepts.definition_short: Angelic invocation names ritual address to angels in medieval texts; it may function as an actor practice in prayer-based ritual books and as an analyst category for the study of theurgic or devotional magic.
concepts.significance: Angelic invocation names ritual address to angels in medieval texts; it may function as an actor practice in prayer-based ritual books and as an analyst category for the study of theurgic or devotional magic.

concepts.label: Demonic Pact
concepts.definition_short: Demonic pact is a theological and legal category used to explain illicit magic as explicit or implicit agreement with demons, while modern historians analyze it as a polemical and juridical tool rather than a transparent description of practice.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Actor and Analyst Term. The demonic pact (pactum cum daemone in Latin; pacte diabolique in French) designates an explicit or implicit agreement between a human being and a demon or the Devil, by which the demon provides services (knowledge, power, material goods, protection) in exchange for the human's submission, worship, or soul. The concept was a cornerstone of medieval and early modern demonological theory, and its application — identifying whether a given magical practice constituted implicit pact — was the central analytical tool through which theologians and inquisitors assessed the moral status of magic.

Theological Development

Augustine of Hippo provided the earliest systematic account of the demonic pact: demons, he argued in De civitate Dei and De divinatione daemonum, respond to human invocation not because they are compelled by magical art but because they desire the worship of human beings diverted from God to themselves. Any consultation of demons — even when framed as a purely technical operation (astrological, divinatory, healing) — involves an implicit compact with beings hostile to human salvation. This framework made the question of pact structural rather than simply intentional: even if the practitioner did not intend to worship a demon, the operation of demonic magic presupposed demonic cooperation that was itself a form of forbidden commerce.

Thomas Aquinas refined this analysis in Summa theologiae II-II, qq. 92–96, developing the distinction between explicit pact (in which the practitioner consciously invokes a demon and requests its service) and implicit pact (in which the practitioner uses means that cannot work through natural causes and therefore presuppose demonic assistance, whether or not the practitioner recognizes this). The concept of implicit pact enormously extended the domain of potentially illicit magic: it meant that any operation using non-natural means (special words, characters, names, images without naturalistic causal explanation) was potentially pactual.

Witch Trials and the Sabbath

The fifteenth-century elaboration of the witches' sabbath added a new dimension: the explicit collective demonic pact, renewed at nocturnal assemblies, through which the witch renounced Christianity and submitted body and soul to the Devil. The Malleus Maleficarum (1486) provided the standard account: the witch makes an explicit pact with the devil, submitting to sexual intercourse with him and receiving in return the power to harm neighbours through maleficia. This version of the pact is a judicial-theological construct rather than simply a theological category, built up through confession (often under torture) and codified in the witch-trial literature of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

Scholarship

Richard Kieckhefer's Magic in the Middle Ages (1989) provides the clearest account of the pact concept in medieval learned discourse. Stuart Clark's Thinking with Demons (1997) analyses it within the broader system of early modern demonological thought. Michael Bailey's Battling Demons (2003) traces the emergence of the sabbath construct in the fifteenth century.
concepts.significance: Demonic pact is a theological and legal category used to explain illicit magic as explicit or implicit agreement with demons, while modern historians analyze it as a polemical and juridical tool rather than a transparent description of practice.

concepts.label: Necromancy
concepts.definition_short: Necromancy is an Analyst Term in much modern scholarship for learned spirit-conjuring practices, although medieval Latin nigromantia often carried broader associations with illicit demonic magic rather than the literal raising of the dead.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Actor Term (historical) and Analyst Term. In its ancient Greek and Roman usage, necromancy (nekromanteia, divination through the dead) designated rituals for consulting the ghosts of the dead, either at their tombs or by summoning them to appear. In medieval Latin usage, nigromantia (often etymologized as "black art" rather than "death-divination") designated demonic conjuration more broadly — the ritual summoning and commanding of demons — regardless of whether the dead were involved. This semantic shift is itself historically significant: medieval learned magicians who practised demonic conjuration called themselves and were called nigromancers.

Medieval Nigromancy

Richard Kieckhefer's analysis of the Munich Manual of demonic magic (Forbidden Rites, 1997) provides the most detailed account of what medieval Latin nigromancy actually involved. The Munich Manual (Clm 849, copied c.1440s) is a practical handbook containing illusionist tricks, love magic, and demonic conjuration proper. The conjuration procedures involve: ritual preparation (fasting, prayer, inscribing a circle), the conjuration formula (invoking divine names and the demon's name to compel appearance), interrogation of the demon, and dismissal. The spirits summoned are not ghosts of the dead but demons — fallen angels — whose hierarchy mirrors the celestial hierarchy of the Solomonic tradition.

The social world of medieval nigromancy, as Kieckhefer analyzes it, was what he calls the "clerical underworld": learned clergymen and university graduates who possessed the Latin literacy necessary to use the manuscripts but whose social position (often minor clergy without secure benefices) left them in economic and social vulnerability that made magical services attractive. Frank Klaassen's systematic survey of English magical manuscripts confirms and refines this picture.

Later Survival

Necromantic procedure — in the older, specifically dead-summoning sense — enjoyed a revival in the Spiritualist movement of the nineteenth century and its derivatives. The late antique Necyomantia tradition, which involved summoning the spirits of the dead at tombs or crossroads, persisted in folk practice and in literary imagination (the Witch of Endor, Lucan's Erictho) long after it ceased to be a living learned practice. Owen Davies's The Haunted: A Social History of Ghosts (2007) provides context for the persistence of ghost-consultation in popular magical practice.
concepts.significance: Necromancy is an Analyst Term in much modern scholarship for learned spirit-conjuring practices, although medieval Latin nigromantia often carried broader associations with illicit demonic magic rather than the literal raising of the dead.

concepts.label: Divination
concepts.definition_short: Divination covers practices for obtaining hidden knowledge, from geomancy and sortilege to astrological judgment; medieval sources classify it variously as natural, superstitious, demonic, or licit depending on method and authority.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Actor and Analyst Term. Divination (from Latin divinare, to foresee, from divinus, divine) designates the attempt to obtain knowledge of hidden, remote, or future events through means other than ordinary sensory experience or rational inference. The category encompasses an enormous range of practices — astrology, geomancy, chiromancy, oneiromancy (dream interpretation), pyromancy, hydromancy, sortilege (casting lots), augury, and consultation of spirits — united by the claim to access knowledge unavailable to ordinary human faculties.

Theological Status

Christian theology took a consistently negative view of divination, on grounds established by Augustine and systematized by Thomas Aquinas. The argument proceeded through several steps: hidden knowledge belongs ultimately to God; creatures (stars, lots, demons) can at best provide signs, not genuine foreknowledge; any appeal to creatures for knowledge that only God possesses constitutes idolatry or demonic pact; ergo all divinatory practices are illicit. This condemnation was nuanced by allowances for natural prognostication through legitimate causal reasoning (the physician who predicts the patient's death from natural signs, the meteorologist who forecasts storms from atmospheric conditions) but these allowances were carefully limited to what natural causes could genuinely produce.

Astrology was the most contested case. Medieval astrologers and their scholastic supporters argued that celestial bodies were genuine natural causes of terrestrial events and that reading their configurations was legitimate natural philosophy, not divination. The Parisian condemnation of 1277 targeted astrological determinism specifically, and the subsequent literature on astrology is largely a negotiation of where natural astrological prediction ends and illicit divination begins.

Geomancy and Related Arts

Geomancy (divination from earth-figures, produced by random marks on sand or dots on paper, combined into sixteen possible figures) was the most widely used learned divinatory system of the medieval period after astrology. Its Arabic origins (translated as ars geomantiae in the twelfth century) gave it the same intellectual prestige as Arabic astrology; it circulated in university and court contexts alongside astrological texts. Don Skemer's Binding Words: Textual Amulets in the Middle Ages (2006) and Sophie Page's work document its manuscript circulation in England and continental Europe.
concepts.significance: Divination covers practices for obtaining hidden knowledge, from geomancy and sortilege to astrological judgment; medieval sources classify it variously as natural, superstitious, demonic, or licit depending on method and authority.

concepts.label: Geomancy
concepts.definition_short: Geomancy is an Actor Term for a learned divinatory art based on figures generated by points or marks and interpreted through structured houses, often circulating with astrology and other clerical arts.
concepts.significance: Geomancy is an Actor Term for a learned divinatory art based on figures generated by points or marks and interpreted through structured houses, often circulating with astrology and other clerical arts.

concepts.significance: Chiromancy is an Actor Term for palmistry or hand-reading, a divinatory practice treated in medieval manuals and often debated within broader classifications of natural signs and illicit prediction.

concepts.label: Charms

concepts.significance: Amulets are objects worn or carried for protection, healing, or influence, frequently combining inscriptions, images, materials, and ritual timing in ways that cross medical, devotional, and magical classifications.

concepts.significance: Talismans are crafted objects intended to mediate celestial, spiritual, or symbolic power; in medieval scholarship the term often overlaps with image magic, astral magic, and Arabic-Latin theories of celestial influence.

concepts.label: Condemned Arts
concepts.definition_short: Condemned arts is a hybrid category for practices classified as illicit by theologians, jurists, pastoral writers, or university authorities, including divination, demonic invocation, image magic, and suspect ritual learning.

concepts.definition_short: Grimoire corpus is an Analyst Term for the unstable family of manuscript and printed ritual books attributed to Solomon, Honorius, Raziel, angels, or ancient sages; the portal must track each text individually rather than treating grimoires as interchangeable.
